Section: Provisional actor rigs and shared control interface > Who owns collision, tools and bounded work?
The desktop simulation owner configures and advances all motors, performs their World queries and applies admitted local effects. Input, UI, scene-tree drawing and Rapier remain main-thread responsibilities. A producer does not receive a live actor, World, collision callback or arbitrary effect footprint. Catalog data and observations cross the boundary as copied values. New rigs use conservative axis-aligned occupancy envelopes around their rotated rectangles. Translation and angular changes are checked in bounded increments; visible legs, tracks, blades, sails and rotors do not become separate collision bodies. A narrower tucked shape may change only through a clear-volume resize. Runtime enclosure stops the actor rather than relocating it through terrain; explicit bounded invalid-spawn recovery remains a separate setup operation. Adhesion requires a sampled current surface and available resource. A rope has a bounded cast, length and obstruction check; losing valid anchor geometry releases the attachment. Neither attachment creates a new native material or makes an unstable cellular structure load-bearing. Rope release, leaps, blasts and ricochets still pass through the motor's collision and final speed bounds. Ripper/Digger excavation and selected blast/blade effects use [`actor_rig_effects.gd`](../../godot/scripts/actor_rig_effects.gd). Its explicit material whitelist and bounded cached footprint protect Wall, composed body masks, out-of-bounds cells and other noneditable materials. The motor checks the path from its center to the requested tool origin, so a muzzle offset cannot start an effect beyond a protected thin wall. Protected cells also occlude the footprint. A changed cell is submitted through the existing owner-local `emit_disc` adapter with radius zero, preserving native cell authority and wake/revision semantics. Blast presentation may place Fire at the admitted center and apply a separate authored actor recoil. This is not native explosion pressure, a conservation-preserving excavation model or a generic Rapier impulse. The [configuration reference](../reference/configuration-reference.md#actor-rig-values) owns exact query, sweep, angular, ray and effect budgets. Exhausting a collision quota refuses further movement; no unbounded catch-up, terrain search, deferred tool queue or inference task is created. Those controller caps do not measure the subsequent native material reactions or the complete desktop frame.

Section: SetA actor controls and legacy policy compatibility > How can a neural policy control the same actor?
**Current interface, future policy consumer:** the movement model consumes a small value command and exposes a bounded observation. Keyboard adaptation and a future neural-network controller must use that same command contract. Their responsibility is to select actions; the actor model remains responsible for admission, acceleration, action timing, energy and collision. The owner-local core methods are `configure_model(StringName) -> bool`, `reset(Vector2)`, `simulate_action(delta, movement, primary, secondary, world)`, `capabilities() -> Dictionary` and `observation() -> PackedFloat32Array`. `movement` is a finite `Vector2` with each component clamped to -1..1. Runner and Crawler ignore y without slowing x; Skimmer additionally limits the vector's magnitude to one so diagonals gain no extra thrust speed. `primary` and `secondary` are held button states interpreted by the selected rule set, with edges retained by the session. These methods are called by the serialized simulation owner; a main-thread or inference worker must use the copied session bridge rather than directly invoking the live actor or passing itself World. Version 1 observations have a fixed 16-float order: | Index | Value | |---:|---| | 0–1 | Position x, y in world cells | | 2–3 | Velocity x, y in cells/second | | 4 | Grounded flag | | 5 | Runtime-enclosed flag | | 6 | Energy fraction | | 7–8 | Primary-ready, secondary-ready flags | | 9 | Remaining action cooldown in seconds | | 10–11 | Primary-active, secondary-active flags | | 12 | Horizontal facing direction | | 13 | Model index: 0 Runner, 1 Skimmer, 2 Crawler | | 14 | Occupancy query count for the last actor update | | 15 | Movement-limited flag | Flag values use 0/1. The entire vector is **not normalized**: absolute position, velocity, timing and query-count fields retain the units above. A training adapter must version its own feature scaling. The session publication pairs each observation row with epoch, simulation tick, model, producer and accepted sequence. The zero-based row index is its actor ID; the vector alone is insufficient to identify a response target. `sequences` reports the latest **admitted** command, which may arrive after the motor last stepped; it is not an applied-action or exact-replay receipt. ACT-002 additionally publishes consumed actions, sequences and edge flags through the [v2 observation contract](actor-rigs.md#identity-freshness-and-consumed-edges); these additive fields do not change the original observation order.

Section: Blacksite Nine
Blacksite Nine is a continuous 3 × 3 industrial complex. Two ruined wastelands flank a fortified research laboratory on the surface. Six buried districts pack worker cells, containment machinery, pressure vessels, crushing equipment and flooded pumps into heavy walls and narrow service passages. Restrained instrument light, dark wiring, corroded metal and deep recesses give the complex its oppressive atmosphere. All nine districts occupy **one 960 × 960 region of one native world**. Crossing a district boundary preserves the player, materials and edits on both sides; **R restores the entire complex**. The separate [Neon Reliquary descent](neon-reliquary-demo.md) retains its four independently installed district scenes and its existing F11 launcher. ![Blacksite Nine rendered as one connected complex](../images/blacksite-nine/blacksite-nine.png)

results.query: How do theme supersets and subsets, exclusions, weighted blends, broad brushstrokes, fine parameters and hard overrides combine in procedural generation?
facts: Concrete descendants are selected through a validated theme DAG; group weight splits among eligible descendants, overlapping selections accumulate, and global exclusions cannot be reintroduced by brushes.

Broad strokes have radius/strength/falloff and parameter edits; controls use canonical priority and ID ordering. Hard parameters and candidate selections apply before generation, and hard material overrides apply last.
The global district_size topology cannot be edited spatially by a theme, brush or hard override; exact material overrides can intentionally block a route.

**Approved owner direction:** create procedural chunk-generation framework/engine candidates that support on-demand interconnected worlds, specific theme subsets and supersets, and blends between them. Section: Procedural generation fields and masked modifiers > How do masks, guidance and hard overrides combine?
A modifier has a stable ID and priority, optional application/exclusion field names, strength, a context predicate and a shape. Shape is either a half-open `bounds` rectangle, a point/polyline with `radius` and `falloff`, or the whole admitted world. Bounds and points are mutually exclusive. Its effective influence is calculated once per initial cell: ```text alpha = application * (1 - exclusion) * strength * context_predicate * shape ``` An omitted application is 1; an omitted exclusion is 0. All factors are normalized. Strength accepts `[0,1]`. Point/polyline geometry uses the existing smooth radial brush influence, with radius in cells and falloff in `0.1..8`. Zero influence is an exact no-op and full influence preserves exact targets. Intermediate geometry and theme edits interpolate; discrete material replacement uses a deterministic global-coordinate selection with the same influence. It does not create a new fractional material state. Each modifier may contain theme weights/exclusions, direct parameter edits, `mappings`, and one material or aggregate output. A mapping names a generation `parameter`, source `field` and valid `low`/`high` target values. Descending maps are valid. A parameter may occur once within the modifier's direct edits and mappings combined. `district_size` remains global-only and cannot be spatially mapped or edited. | Stage | Evaluation and authority | |---|---| | Initial proposal | Original theme/brush/parameter/candidate controls establish the immutable context | | Scalar graph and masks | Evaluate every field once; capture every modifier influence once | | Theme guidance | Apply all modifier theme blends in ascending priority, then lexical ID | | Geometry guidance | Reblend theme parameters and old brush parameters; apply modifier direct edits and mappings in the same stable order | | Hard geometry and raster | Reapply hard parameter/candidate overrides, then produce the updated candidate material | | Feature modules | Run prepared samplers under bounds, field masks and declared dependency order | | Material guidance | Apply material/aggregate modifier outputs using their original captured influences | | Connecting geometry | Restore the shared network, then apply explicit guide paths | | Hard material | Apply final exact material overrides | Array order never acts as priority. Higher priority and then later lexical ID win overlapping edits within their stage. Global theme exclusions remain eligibility constraints under all later theme guidance. A wholly excluded modifier target rejects compilation; a group that retains eligible descendants can still resolve. Hard parameter controls remain exact after guidance, and final hard materials can deliberately block routes or replace any earlier output. Feature instances add `application`, `exclusion` and `strength` to the existing module schema.

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > What is the control precedence?
The evaluation order is stable and independent of manifest array insertion order. IDs are required; duplicate IDs within a layer are rejected. For brushes, paths, modifiers and hard overrides, lower `priority` runs first, with lexical ID as the tie-break. Later values win. Moving an item in a JSON array is not a hidden priority control. | Order | Control | Meaning | |---|---|---| | 1 | Global parameters and resolved theme parameters | Establish the selected candidate's initial shape and palette distribution | | 2 | Broad polyline brushstrokes | Blend theme weights and selected shape parameters using radius, strength and falloff | | 3 | Hard parameter/candidate overrides | Assign exact values within a half-open world-space rectangle | | 4 | Initial raster and context | Capture the original proposed material, surface and route context before later changes | | 5 | Scalar fields and modifier influence | Evaluate the field DAG once and capture each modifier's application/exclusion/context/shape mask | | 6 | Masked theme and geometry guidance | Apply all theme blends; reblend theme/old brush parameters; apply direct edits and mappings; reapply hard geometry controls and rasterize | | 7 | Prepared feature modules | Add or carve structured zones in dependency order, clipped to bounds and optional field masks | | 8 | Masked material or aggregate modifiers | Use the original captured influence to select discrete existing material IDs | | 9 | Shared network and explicit guide paths | Reserve connective space after modules/modifiers; a guide may carve Empty or paint another material | | 10 | Hard material overrides | Force the final material, including intentionally blocking a route | Schema 3 inserts accepted semantic shell/interior/aggregate proposals between steps 6 and 7 and restores explicit semantic passages after step 9. Existing native modules and material modifiers can therefore contribute to semantic places, while final hard material overrides still win. The hierarchy's final-cell route report observes that complete stack and reports any blocked passage; it does not reinterpret a hard override as optional. Recipes without grammar retain the table's preceding behavior. The [field/modifier contract](procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) defines the two guidance stages, mapping endpoints and immutable context. No earlier modifier can change the context observed by a later modifier. Recipes without new controls retain their old material behavior; fixed legacy hashes cover all three candidates in four signed chunks. Brush points are world-space `[x,y]` pairs. A single point is a dab; multiple points form a polyline. Influence uses distance to the nearest segment, a smooth radial falloff raised

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > How are themes, subsets and supersets resolved?
The recipe catalogue is a validated directed acyclic graph. A theme has an ID, zero or more parents, optional typed parameter edits, a `concrete` flag and a four-material palette. Groups expand into their concrete descendants; concrete themes are the eligible emitted palettes. A concrete theme may belong to multiple groups. Unknown parents, cycles, duplicate IDs, invalid materials and oversized catalogues are rejected before any job exists. The built-in hierarchy is: | Group | Concrete descendants | |---|---| | `natural` | `dry_cavern`, `wet_cavern`, `basalt`, `garden` | | `built` | `industrial`, `ruins`, `garden` | | `world` | All six concrete themes | `garden` intentionally belongs to both `natural` and `built`. The initial catalogue can be replaced with an explicit `catalogue` in a native recipe or Godot manifest. Palette roles are `rock`, `surface`, `accent` and `fluid`; material IDs remain discrete. Stable rock construction uses block materials, not movable `Stone`. Selection uses `themes.weights`, a mapping from group or concrete ID to a nonnegative weight. Each selected group's mass is divided equally among its eligible concrete descendants. Overlapping selections accumulate, then normalize. For example, a group containing A/B with weight 3 and an unrelated C with weight 1 resolves to A=0.375, B=0.375, C=0.25. Selecting the A/B group with weight 1 and A with weight 1 resolves to A=0.75, B=0.25. A repeated selector ID is invalid. `themes.exclude` removes an entire group or a concrete theme before normalization. Global exclusions remain hard eligibility constraints in every brush and masked theme modifier. Neither can reintroduce an excluded descendant. An all-zero or entirely excluded selection is invalid; generation never silently substitutes a fallback theme. At a cell, spatial brushes and masked theme guidance blend normalized theme weights. A uniform hash of a warped world-space patch selects a concrete palette from the effective weights. This produces coherent material regions; weights are preferences across regions, not exact material-area quotas in an arbitrary finite crop. The fallback for floating-point accumulation can only select a positive, eligible weight. Theme parameter edits inherit through parents in sorted parent order, with the child applied last. Multiple-parent conflicts therefore have explicit deterministic precedence; use a child edit to make a required value unambiguous. Palette fields belong to each concrete theme and are not implicitly inherited. Effective theme parameters blend from an eligible reference plus weighted differences, preserving identical minimum values exactly rather than rounding a one-cell wall to zero.

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > How do chunks connect without generating neighbors?
Every field is sampled at global coordinates. Seeded lattice values depend on seed, coordinates and an algorithm lane, not a mutable PRNG sequence. Changing request order, slicing a job into different cell budgets, or partitioning the same region into different chunk sizes therefore leaves its material cells unchanged for the same effective recipe. Flow Network and District Grammar divide the plane into fixed macrocells. Each cell has a seeded interior hub. An edge's port is derived from a canonical edge coordinate and axis; its two owners independently obtain the same port. Each hub connects to all four edge ports. No recursive neighbor request, global graph construction, speculative edge negotiation or neighbor-residency check is needed. The shared skeleton is carved after feature modules and material modifiers so their ordinary walls do not seal it. An independent regression fills the region with solid Metal and requires a four-neighbor Empty component across a negative-coordinate 2x2 macrocell region to reach every outer side. The current guarantee is a deterministic raster connection in one unchanged recipe. It does not guarantee that independently edited recipes meet, that a large player fits every passage, or that a passage containing later simulation material remains traversable. Explicit hard material/candidate changes may alter connectivity by design. The workbench replaces its complete preview revision after an edit, avoiding a mixture of old and new generated chunks. Native World supports wider signed coordinates. This generator deliberately accepts only complete chunks inside `[-2^40,2^40)` cell coordinates: brush geometry uses doubles, and out-of-domain requests must refuse rather than alias distant positions. Negative coordinates use mathematical floor division. A job must fit the entire chunk in that domain before allocating its output.

Section: Procedural generation fields and masked modifiers > Which context is available to guidance and sculpting?
The generator first resolves the original theme selection, old polyline brushes and hard parameter/candidate overrides, then rasterizes that initial candidate. It captures context at this point, before field-guided changes, structural modules, material/aggregate modifiers, connective carving, explicit paths or hard material overrides. All fields and modifier predicates for the cell see this same capture. | Channel | Initial proposal meaning | |---|---| | `occupied` | 1 for any non-Empty material, otherwise 0 | | `solid` | 1 only for the existing `MaterialState::Solid`; Powder is occupied but not solid | | `fluid` | 1 only for the existing `MaterialState::Liquid` | | `material` | Exact existing material ID, consumed by a `material` field or predicate | | `depth` | Downward-positive `y - surface(x)` using the original Strata surface formula | | `slope` | Absolute surface-height difference across x−1/x+1, divided by two; one-sided at the admitted coordinate boundary | | `route` | Binary initial shared-network membership for Flow Network/District Grammar; zero for Strata | The analytic surface uses the original effective `surface_y` and `relief`, even when the candidate is District Grammar. Slope recomputes the original theme, brush and hard-parameter state at each neighboring surface sample. Consequently an authored height brush can contribute slope even with zero noise relief. It does not read neighboring material occupancy or recursively evaluate fields. A modifier's `context` predicate is `any`, `empty`, `occupied`, `solid`, `fluid` or `material`; only the last requires `context_material`. For example, an occupied-only carving modifier can remove initial terrain without a later empty-only modifier treating that new hole as initially empty. Material added by a module does not retroactively change a field mask. This fixed observation point prevents order-dependent context feedback and keeps cross-chunk sampling local. The standalone graph accepts a copied `FieldContext` from a native caller. Binary channels must be finite in `[0,1]`; material IDs must exist; absolute depth and nonnegative slope are bounded by `2 * 2^40`. That value interface is not a live World-query hook. A future adapter supplying live observations would need its own immutable snapshot, revision and scheduling contract.

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > What is implemented?
**Current candidate source, GEN-001 / [#163](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/163) and GEN-002 / [#171](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/171):** three CPU procedural generators share one immutable recipe, theme hierarchy, spatial control stack and extensible native feature registry. They produce actual material IDs for signed-coordinate chunks. Generation is separate from simulation: it does not tick materials, query a mutable World, call Godot, request neighboring chunks or share a mutable random generator. The [public native API](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) and [implementation](../../native/src/world_generation.cpp) own these semantics. GEN-002 adds named structured-noise/finite-curve fields, scalar sidechains, masked context-aware guidance and sculpting, aggregate material recipes and paced diagnostic channels. The focused [fields and modifiers contract](procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) owns those controls, immutable initial context and finite Hilbert/Morton scope. GEN-003 / [#190](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/190) adds explicit schema-2 [typed spatial functions](procedural-typed-spatial-fields.md): signed distance/vector/category values, transformed/derived geometry, reusable parameter subgraphs, structured seeds, finite adjacency assignments and world-aligned multiresolution sampling. The retained scalar graph remains separately defined; typed spatial functions have no per-cell initial-context input. Only explicit normalized `spatial:<id>` outputs may drive existing masks and mappings. GEN-004 / [#191](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/191) adds explicit schema-3 [hierarchical semantic plans](procedural-hierarchical-generation.md). Finite canonical regions own nested places and cross-chunk structures; stable rule/slot IDs, placement constraints, matched sockets, explicit loops/service trunks and final-raster route reports precede ordinary chunk publication. Selected immutable semantic geometries may feed the typed graph. The hierarchy does not add World streaming or replace final hard material authority. | Candidate | Generated structure | Suitable starting point | |---|---|---| | `strata` | Smoothly varying surface, domain-warped caves, strata, deposits and material-specific deep fill | Organic terrain, underground spaces and theme transitions | | `flow_network` | Strata plus a connected macrocell hub/port network, carved after structural modules | Interconnected passages, service routes and excavation networks | | `district_grammar` | Global room/floor lattice with repeated doors and accents, plus the same hub/port network | Dense urban interiors, industrial districts and structured construction | ![Actual native generation with the same authored controls across the three candidates](../figures/worldgen-candidates.png) Seed 314159; each panel covers 512 by 384 cells at origin `[-256,0]`. Reproduce the material pixels with `make worldgen-demo`. This is generation output, before simulation. Every candidate consumes the same brushes, paths, overrides and feature instances. A hard candidate override can choose another generator inside a rectangular zone. This is deliberately a set of provisional algorithms, not a selected production world style or a proof of useful player navigation. In particular, generator connectivity does not establish actor clearance, gravity traversal or fluid equilibrium; the existing material and actor owners retain those semantics. **Current authoring surface:** the separate [worldgen workbench](../../godot/worldgen_workbench.tscn) previews generated material pixels and performs bounded demand generation while panning.

Section: Hierarchical procedural places and structural routes > How do I author and inspect the multi-district example?
Load [`hierarchy-multi-district.json`](../../examples/worldgen/hierarchy-multi-district.json) through the Workbench hierarchy example control or `CyberWorldGenerator.configure`. It covers `[-128,-128,256,256]` cells in four canonical 128-cell regions, using 64-cell storage chunks. Each region contains semantic theme subdivisions, one 104×72 foundry, a 64×66 gallery, a machinery bay, an inspection dais with floor and wall constraints, a floor-mounted pump, a ceiling console and two embedded dais lights. The machinery bay occupies 22.22% of its foundry. Neighbor, separation, service, exact multiplicity, socket and occupancy constraints are authored data. The profile uses the shared finite assignment solver for district theme blends, order-1 Hilbert-ranked foundry candidates and detail placement, a real theme-boundary preference for a marker, explicit primary routes and secondary loops, a four-site curve-ordered service tour and straight service/liquid trunks, a prepared vault module, a weathered aggregate shell and a typed distance mask around an exported tour loop. Its Strata base is composed with Flow Network and District Grammar overrides. `get_semantic_plan()` exposes the hierarchy and receipts; `inspect_cell()` reports contribution provenance; `validate_routes()` reports the declared final-cell traversal and support-contact qualifications separately. The example deliberately places its compact apparatus away from both semantic passage footprints and the existing candidate macro network for the authored seed. Its retained qualification and the footprint inspection are recorded in the [dated audit](../audits/2026-10-21-gen004-hierarchical-generation.md). For a new place, choose its canonical region/window and stable rule IDs first. Declare parent-relative candidate rectangles and exact counts, then add hard requirements and socket apertures. Give higher-priority scopes to required supports or theme areas. Add preferences only after a valid hard layout exists. Use explicit omission fallback only when absence is an acceptable authored outcome. Inspect semantic receipts before tuning masks/materials, then recheck final raster routes after any hard override. Save accepted JSON with full numeric precision using the existing Workbench configuration path. [`grammar-v1.schema.json`](../../examples/worldgen/schemas/grammar-v1.schema.json) is the versioned JSON authoring schema for the `grammar` member of a schema-3 recipe. The native compiler additionally checks relational, geometric, type, cycle, work and memory invariants that JSON Schema cannot establish. The [build guide](../operations/local-build-and-validation.md#hierarchical-generation-example-and-acceptance) routes executable tests. Human movement feel, Windows/browser behavior and render throughput require their own dated execution evidence.

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > How does generated content enter the native simulation?
`World::install_generated_chunk(chunk, row_major_materials)` is an additive native C++ owner operation. It requires exactly the World's configured chunk area, checks all materials and coordinate arithmetic, refuses failed/in-progress Worlds, checks transient occupancy and capacity, and rejects **any already resident chunk**, including pre-reserved empty storage or cells edited and then erased. Thus generation cannot mistake an excavated resident area for never-generated terrain. Even an all-Empty payload establishes residence. After admission, ordinary `World::set` initialization supplies material-local state, configured full Water mass, epochs, dirty/wake/hard-surface metadata and discovery observations. No generated temperature/state bytes, Rapier bodies or new material semantics are invented. The owner may then simulate the chunk using the existing native rules. Invalid input/capacity/occupancy refusals produce no partial material installation. Initial allocation may throw before installation. The raw installer takes materials, not a generator/session receipt. Its caller must first check `Generator::accepts`, match chunk size, and own the World/reset lifetime. `World::clear` permits new chunks again; an old result from a previous World session must be discarded by the coordinator even if the recipe is unchanged. No automatic world-session receipt protocol or live Godot simulation attachment is claimed by this primitive. It must never run concurrently with World ticks, queries or rendering publication.

Section: Data ownership and lifetimes > How may generated content enter cell authority?
**Current GEN-001/GEN-002 source:** the generation job API and supplied module context provide no mutable World, scene-tree or Rapier state. The [generation contract](../systems/procedural-world-generation.md) separates immutable recipe/revision receipts from the destination World's lifetime. `Generator::accepts` validates the former; the caller must also establish the current World/reset session and hold exclusive ownership before invoking [`World::install_generated_chunk`](../../native/src/world.cpp). Installation prevalidates one complete material span before allocating/writing, requires an absent destination chunk and uses existing native mutation defaults. Even a reserved empty or edited-then-cleared resident chunk is protected from regeneration. Failed Worlds, in-tick calls, invalid payloads, capacity/coordinate failure and overlapping transient occupancy are explicit refusals. This method is a loading/setup boundary primitive; it supplies no background World owner, automatic resident eviction or reset-session manager. The opt-in workbench only previews copied proposals and never calls it on the sandbox World. GEN-002 scalar context observes the initial procedural candidate, including its old brushes and hard geometry controls, before any masked modifier or module. It does not borrow live World material or infer player edits from empty preview cells. Diagnostic floats are job-owned and receipt-bound, then copied into the workbench cache; changing inspection channels retires that cache. The [field/modifier contract](../systems/procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) owns this immutable-context and diagnostic lifecycle. GEN-003 schema-2 [`SpatialGraph`](../../native/include/cybersand/generation_typed_fields.hpp) adds immutable typed functions beside that retained context graph. It never resamples `FieldContext` as if it contained neighboring observations. Route and feature geometry is copied; finite region assignments finish preparation before publication. Each caller or job owns its bounded sampling scratch. Typed diagnostics preserve signed values, vector components and exact categorical identities; the chunk receipt binds both payload and type/unit metadata, and failure/cancellation publishes neither materials nor diagnostics. The [typed contract](../systems/procedural-typed-spatial-fields.md) owns these lifetimes and cache identities. Future grammar, authoring and streaming owners may consume the interfaces without gaining mutable cell access.

Section: World storage and interest region > What does fresh generated-chunk admission protect?
**Current:** [`World::install_generated_chunk`](../../native/src/world.cpp) accepts exactly one row-major material span whose dimensions match the native storage chunk. It checks the whole payload, coordinate arithmetic, capacity, transient occupancy and current World/tick state before mutation. Every resident chunk is refused, including empty reservations and chunks whose edits were later cleared. Accepted cells use ordinary native initialization, activity and dirty tracking; generation is not an alternate material simulation. The caller owns recipe/receipt validation and the destination World/reset-session check. The material-only admission method is not proof that a stale job still belongs to a newly reset World. Use the [ownership contract](../architecture/data-ownership-and-lifetimes.md) before connecting it to a future streaming controller. The current generation workbench has no live sandbox installer and its preview cache evicts only copied previews. Context-aware sculpting reads immutable initial generator context; aggregate recipes produce existing material IDs. Neither observes resident player changes, changes the installer guard nor adds optional simulation field storage.

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > How do chunks connect without generating neighbors?
Every field is sampled at global coordinates. Seeded lattice values depend on seed, coordinates and an algorithm lane, not a mutable PRNG sequence. Changing request order, slicing a job into different cell budgets, or partitioning the same region into different chunk sizes therefore leaves its material cells unchanged for the same effective recipe. Flow Network and District Grammar divide the plane into fixed macrocells. Each cell has a seeded interior hub. An edge's port is derived from a canonical edge coordinate and axis; its two owners independently obtain the same port. Each hub connects to all four edge ports. No recursive neighbor request, global graph construction, speculative edge negotiation or neighbor-residency check is needed. The shared skeleton is carved after feature modules and material modifiers so their ordinary walls do not seal it. An independent regression fills the region with solid Metal and requires a four-neighbor Empty component across a negative-coordinate 2x2 macrocell region to reach every outer side. The current guarantee is a deterministic raster connection in one unchanged recipe. It does not guarantee that independently edited recipes meet, that a large player fits every passage, or that a passage containing later simulation material remains traversable. Explicit hard material/candidate changes may alter connectivity by design. The workbench replaces its complete preview revision after an edit, avoiding a mixture of old and new generated chunks. Native World supports wider signed coordinates. This generator deliberately accepts only complete chunks inside `[-2^40,2^40)` cell coordinates: brush geometry uses doubles, and out-of-domain requests must refuse rather than alias distant positions. Negative coordinates use mathematical floor division. A job must fit the entire chunk in that domain before allocating its output.

Section: Module boundaries > Where should new code belong? > How do advanced generation modules extend the engine?
**Current GEN-001/GEN-002 source:** the native [`ModuleRegistry`](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) resolves versioned factories before generation. Factories prepare immutable samplers outside simulation ticks; a sampler receives the current coordinate, immutable effective parameters/palette and previous proposed material. It returns at most one material for that cell. The generator clips the module's declared rectangle, orders dependencies and validates the result before publishing a chunk. The independent [`FieldGraph`](../../native/include/cybersand/generation_fields.hpp) evaluates a bounded scalar DAG from coordinates and copied initial context. It has no custom callback or simulation dependency. The generator uses those values to mask modules and guide themes, parameters or discrete aggregate output. Aggregate definitions resolve existing material IDs; they do not define new MaterialRules. The [field/modifier contract](../systems/procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) owns fixed observation order, finite curve scope and graph budgets. GEN-003 adds a separate immutable [`SpatialGraph`](../../native/include/cybersand/generation_typed_fields.hpp) for signed scalars, distances, vectors, exact categories and booleans. Typed transforms and derivatives resample only immutable absolute-coordinate inputs; they cannot read the scalar graph's per-cell context or mutable World storage. [`generation_spatial`](../../native/include/cybersand/generation_spatial.hpp) owns bounded Peano/lattice/Poisson primitives, copied geometry and the single finite region-assignment solver. Explicit normalized outputs feed the existing mask interface; the [typed contract](../systems/procedural-typed-spatial-fields.md) and [operator inventory](../reference/procedural-spatial-operators.md) own the spatial computation boundary. **Current GEN-004 source:** the separate immutable [`GrammarPlan`](../../native/include/cybersand/generation_grammar.hpp) prepares a bounded hierarchy, canonical boundary ports, explicit routes and constraint receipts before rasterization. It uses the shared region-assignment solver and exports selected immutable geometry to typed fields without a reverse field-to-grammar dependency. The generator applies feature proposals, modules and modifiers, restores required passages, then retains final hard overrides. It qualifies that complete material stack against a declared geometric route profile and separate static-solid-contact profile before publishing the recipe. This planning and inspection boundary does not own simulation admission or actor navigation; the [hierarchy contract](../systems/procedural-hierarchical-generation.md) owns its finite scope, deterministic identities and limits. Modules are trusted cooperative C++ code: declared logical cost bounds admission, while the host cannot sandbox an arbitrary callback or enforce its execution time. The workbench selects registered modules through recipes; it does not load arbitrary executable libraries from a recipe. Native World remains the sole cell authority and accepts a completed material span only through its separate exclusive-owner admission method. See the [generation contract](../systems/procedural-world-generation.md) and [lifetimes](data-ownership-and-lifetimes.md).

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > How are advanced feature modules loaded and extended?
A manifest module instance names a registered factory ID and exact version, world-space bounds, numeric parameter map, instance ID, priority and optional `after` dependency IDs. Optional `application`/`exclusion` field references and `strength` control its influence inside those bounds. The native registry resolves the factory and prepares a shared immutable sampler during recipe compilation, before ordinary generation. Each job invokes that sampler only inside its instance bounds. A sampler receives the current global cell coordinate, seed, effective parameters, palette and previous material; it can return one material or decline the cell. | Built-in factory | Preparation / generated feature | Optional integer parameters | |---|---|---| | `arcology` v1 | Multistory floors, bays, shell/windows, service shaft, cables and lights | `bay_width=48`, `floor_height=32`, `wall=3`, `shaft_width=10` | | `vault` v1 | A deterministic spanning-tree maze of connected rooms, prepared once and then sampled in constant work | `cell_size=32`, `wall=2`, `door_width=8` | | `aqueduct` v1 | Repeated arched masonry supports, deck and fluid trough | `span=64`, `deck_height=24`, `wall=3`, `channel_depth=6` | Vault bounds must be multiples of `cell_size`, with at most 64 rooms per axis and 4096 rooms total. Its DFS preparation visits a fixed finite room graph; generation does not rerun the maze solver per chunk. Two outer doorways join the connected interior. Arcology validates that its shaft/shell fit. Aqueduct validates room for the trough and arches. Unknown keys and invalid geometry reject compilation. Dependencies refer to instance IDs, not neighboring chunk outputs. The compiler uses stable topological order; among currently ready instances, priority and ID decide order. Missing/self/duplicate dependencies and cycles are rejected. The order allows one module to refine a previous module's material in overlapping bounds without giving it access to another job or mutable World. To add a native algorithm, implement `FeatureSampler::sample`, register a `ModuleFactory` with `ModuleRegistry::add`, and compile the recipe with that registry. The factory can precompute BSP rooms, a bounded constraint solution, architectural supports, a transport graph or a sampled computational field. Keep prepared state owned by the returned sampler, const/thread-safe for concurrent jobs, and invalidate the module version whenever its output algorithm changes. Registered factory versions and prepared inputs participate in recipe identity. This is a **trusted native module ABI within the source build**, with runtime factory registration and manifest-driven loading of prepared instances. The Godot binding currently supplies the built-in registry. JSON imports do not download or execute scripts, load arbitrary DLLs, or install new C++ code. results.query: Does a Hilbert or Morton generation field make one continuous infinite corridor, and do its tiles change at negative chunk boundaries?
facts: Hilbert guarantees edge adjacency between consecutive ranks inside a finite power-of-two tile only; repeated tiles do not promise a continuous infinite Hilbert curve. Morton interleaves coordinates and successive ranks need not share an edge.
Orders 1 through 20 and integer cell sizes 1 through 4096 use signed floor tiling at absolute coordinates, independently of the output chunk partition.
The separately defined macrocell hub/port network owns interconnected procedural routes. Curve fields can guide masks, parameters or material variation without replacing that network.

Section: Procedural generation fields and masked modifiers > What do Hilbert and Morton guarantee at signed chunk boundaries?
Curve tiles have side `2^order`, where `order` is an integer from 1 through 20. Each local curve cell covers `cell_size` world cells per axis, an integer from 1 through 4096. Origin coordinates are integer cells. At the maximum settings, one tile spans `2^32` world cells per axis; intermediate address arithmetic is wide enough for that extent. `curve_address(kind, x, y, order, cell_size, origin_x, origin_y)` returns signed tile coordinates, local unsigned coordinates and a local rank. Floor division assigns negative cells consistently. `curve_index` and `curve_point` convert between local coordinates and rank without sampling any neighbor. Scalar curve fields divide the rank by `2^(2*order)-1`, retaining exact endpoint values. Hilbert order 1 visits `(0,0)`, `(0,1)`, `(1,1)`, `(1,0)`. Consecutive Hilbert ranks share an edge **within the same finite tile**. Tiling repeats that local addressing pattern; there is no promised continuous infinite Hilbert path between tiles. Morton interleaves x bits in even lanes and y bits in odd lanes; successive Morton ranks need not share an edge. A Morton field is therefore a spatial ordering control, not an automatically connected corridor. The generator's separately defined macrocell hub/port network owns interconnected routes. Curve fields may guide material seams, masks, variation or parameter mapping without replacing that connectivity contract. Both curve ranks and resulting material proposals stay independent of output chunk size, including partitions and brush shapes crossing negative coordinates. Samples must lie inside `[-2^40,2^40)`; curve and field origin parameters accept both endpoints of `[-2^40,2^40]`. Out-of-domain requests and invalid curve ranks, local coordinates, orders or cell sizes reject explicitly.

Section: Chunk, tile, and buffer model > How does a generation chunk relate to simulation geometry?
**Current GEN-001/GEN-002 source:** an opt-in [`generation::Recipe`](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) chooses the square output partition for a procedural proposal. Sampling uses global coordinates, so requesting neighboring chunks in a different order or partitioning the same region does not change its material proposals. Generation neither runs the scheduler nor reads which neighbors happen to be resident. Flow Network and District Grammar derive shared macrocell ports from seed and global topology independently of output chunk size. Theme/brush changes cannot change that topology parameter locally; modules run before the connective skeleton is restored, while a final hard material override can intentionally close a route. These are generated layout relationships, not simulation write domains or new cellular transfer rules. The [generation contract](../systems/procedural-world-generation.md) owns their bounds/precedence; World admission separately requires its configured chunk size and a previously absent destination. Finite Hilbert/Morton tiles, aggregate grains, mask shapes and output chunks are separate spatial partitions. GEN-002 addresses each from absolute coordinates with signed floor division; changing output chunk size does not reset a field tile or grain. Consecutive Hilbert ranks connect only within one finite tile, while Morton ranks are not a continuous route. Neither substitutes for the generator's macrocell port network or the simulation scheduler's write domains. See the [field/curve contract](../systems/procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md). GEN-004 adds a finite authored window of canonical world-zero region addresses. Its `region_size` defines semantic ownership independently of output chunks; changing that grid size intentionally changes the semantic identity namespace. A region-owned building can span many storage chunks. Neighboring regions derive the same shared boundary socket without observing chunk residency, and explicit passages and utility routes carry the cross-region connection. The [hierarchy contract](../systems/procedural-hierarchical-generation.md) distinguishes these finite plans from future persistent-world streaming.

Section: Typed spatial fields, transforms and reusable generation graphs > What do Peano, Voronoi, Delaunay and Poisson guarantee?
The Peano operator extends the retained finite Hilbert/Morton controls with a ternary square traversal. Side length is `3^order`, `order=1..12`; each local cell spans `cell_size=1..4096` world cells. Rank and inverse are bijections. Consecutive Peano ranks share an edge **inside one finite tile**. Signed tile addressing uses floor division. No infinite path or physical route is promised between independently repeated tiles; authored routes and the generator's shared-network controls retain that separate role. Voronoi seeds use one deterministically jittered point in each world-aligned lattice tile. `spacing` is `1..1,048,576` cells and `jitter` is `[0,1]`. A fixed 5×5 candidate search suffices for the nearest point because the containing tile always supplies a seed within `sqrt(2)*spacing`. Equal distances choose the lexicographically smaller signed seed coordinate. Region identity retains both seed coordinates and a stable graph domain; it does not pack an unbounded address into a floating-point number. `voronoi_distance` returns nearest-seed distance. `voronoi_boundary` measures distance to the nearest competing Voronoi boundary under its bounded 7×7 competitor search. `delaunay_degree` exposes the size of the positive-length Voronoi-face dual. The lower-level neighborhood API additionally returns incident neighbors/positions and distance to the owner's incident segments. Co-circular zero-length diagonal edges are deliberately omitted; a square lattice therefore has four face neighbors rather than an arbitrary triangulation diagonal. This is the documented Delaunay-derived structure. Poisson-style seeds use deterministic Matérn-II priority rejection. Each lattice tile owns one candidate. It survives only if no candidate within the authored radius has a lower `(priority, signed ID)` ordering. Rejected candidates still compete; acceptance never recursively asks whether a neighbor survived. Radius must be positive and no greater than twice the lattice spacing. Candidate ownership is half-open and independent of requested chunks. The query radius is `R=search_cells*spacing`, with `search_cells=1..4`. `poisson_found` reports whether an accepted seed lies strictly inside R. `poisson_distance` returns the nearest accepted distance capped at R. A `poisson_region` identity must be interpreted together with `poisson_found` when no candidate is found. This bounded selection gives hard minimum separation, not a guaranteed globally nearest seed, maximal packing or a measured blue-noise spectral guarantee.

Section: Hierarchical procedural places and structural routes > How are sockets, routes and finite curves used structurally?
A socket has an authored ID, route type, outward direction, integer edge offset, odd aperture width, required flag and attachment policy. Width and offset must fit the selected feature edge. Automatic attachment selects the nearest compatible predeclared regional route deterministically, checks passage width, creates an opposite-facing matching socket and an explicit connector that first exits along the authored normal. Shared boundary ports remain canonical records. Unsupported or unmatched required connections reject the plan. Hilbert, Morton and Peano are finite orderings of authored candidate addresses `order_x/order_y`. Their ranks affect candidate placement, progressive density and retained inspection/tour order. They can order declared district subdivisions or apparatus positions without array-order dependence. With `curve_services`, a bounded service tour visits finite curve sites in rank order and constructs explicit orthogonal material trunk edges between them, joined to the straight regional service. Hilbert/Morton use at most sixteen sites and Peano nine; a Morton jump is an authored L-shaped route, not an inferred adjacent step. Curve ranks never replace the explicit edge geometry used by hub arms, loops, utility trunks and socket connectors. Hilbert/Peano adjacency holds only inside their documented finite domains; Morton may jump. A sorted list of features alone is not a physical route.

The opt-in [workbench](../../godot/scripts/worldgen_workbench.gd) has named field editing from the native kind catalogue, aggregate component controls, modifier editing, application/exclusion selectors, context filters and field-to-parameter mapping. Canvas tools carve, paint materials/aggregates or add masked parameter and theme guidance. Bounded modifiers can be translated/scaled; complete JSON remains available for combinations and exact values. Inspecting a ready preview cell can select its material as a future initial-context filter. ![Rendered aggregate authoring controls and native material preview](../figures/worldgen-aggregate-workbench.png) This Linux software-OpenGL capture shows the accepted aggregate editor and copied native material preview. The layout was reviewed at the normal and compact window sizes recorded in the [audit](../audits/2026-10-18-gen002-fields-and-aggregates.md); it is not a target-GPU performance measurement. The diagnostic picker chooses materials or one accepted field/modifier/module channel. Changing the channel retires the preview work and cache before requesting replacement data. Packets contain copied `PackedByteArray` materials and optional `PackedFloat32Array` diagnostics. The UI checks current identity, completion coordinate, channel, shape and normalized values before display; it does not recompute the native receipt. Grayscale diagnostic textures are derived views of those copied floats. No preview or sculpting command installs into the live sandbox. The [local build guide](../operations/local-build-and-validation.md) owns runnable commands for the native suites, workbench tests and exact profile renderer. Independent [field tests](../../native/tests/test_generation_fields.cpp) and [modifier tests](../../native/tests/test_generation_modifiers.cpp) cover analytical values, finite-curve inverses/adjacency, signed partitions, canonical ordering, immutable context, exclusions, hard authority, aggregate IDs, failures and receipts. Section: Procedural generation fields and masked modifiers > How do masks, guidance and hard overrides combine?
A modifier has a stable ID and priority, optional application/exclusion field names, strength, a context predicate and a shape. Shape is either a half-open `bounds` rectangle, a point/polyline with `radius` and `falloff`, or the whole admitted world. Bounds and points are mutually exclusive. Its effective influence is calculated once per initial cell: ```text alpha = application * (1 - exclusion) * strength * context_predicate * shape ``` An omitted application is 1; an omitted exclusion is 0. All factors are normalized. Strength accepts `[0,1]`. Point/polyline geometry uses the existing smooth radial brush influence, with radius in cells and falloff in `0.1..8`. Zero influence is an exact no-op and full influence preserves exact targets. Intermediate geometry and theme edits interpolate; discrete material replacement uses a deterministic global-coordinate selection with the same influence. It does not create a new fractional material state. Each modifier may contain theme weights/exclusions, direct parameter edits, `mappings`, and one material or aggregate output. A mapping names a generation `parameter`, source `field` and valid `low`/`high` target values. Descending maps are valid. A parameter may occur once within the modifier's direct edits and mappings combined. `district_size` remains global-only and cannot be spatially mapped or edited. | Stage | Evaluation and authority | |---|---| | Initial proposal | Original theme/brush/parameter/candidate controls establish the immutable context | | Scalar graph and masks | Evaluate every field once; capture every modifier influence once | | Theme guidance | Apply all modifier theme blends in ascending priority, then lexical ID | | Geometry guidance | Reblend theme parameters and old brush parameters; apply modifier direct edits and mappings in the same stable order | | Hard geometry and raster | Reapply hard parameter/candidate overrides, then produce the updated candidate material | | Feature modules | Run prepared samplers under bounds, field masks and declared dependency order | | Material guidance | Apply material/aggregate modifier outputs using their original captured influences | | Connecting geometry | Restore the shared network, then apply explicit guide paths | | Hard material | Apply final exact material overrides | Array order never acts as priority. Higher priority and then later lexical ID win overlapping edits within their stage. Global theme exclusions remain eligibility constraints under all later theme guidance. A wholly excluded modifier target rejects compilation; a group that retains eligible descendants can still resolve. Hard parameter controls remain exact after guidance, and final hard materials can deliberately block routes or replace any earlier output. Feature instances add `application`, `exclusion` and `strength` to the existing module schema.

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > What is the control precedence?
The evaluation order is stable and independent of manifest array insertion order. IDs are required; duplicate IDs within a layer are rejected. For brushes, paths, modifiers and hard overrides, lower `priority` runs first, with lexical ID as the tie-break. Later values win. Moving an item in a JSON array is not a hidden priority control. | Order | Control | Meaning | |---|---|---| | 1 | Global parameters and resolved theme parameters | Establish the selected candidate's initial shape and palette distribution | | 2 | Broad polyline brushstrokes | Blend theme weights and selected shape parameters using radius, strength and falloff | | 3 | Hard parameter/candidate overrides | Assign exact values within a half-open world-space rectangle | | 4 | Initial raster and context | Capture the original proposed material, surface and route context before later changes | | 5 | Scalar fields and modifier influence | Evaluate the field DAG once and capture each modifier's application/exclusion/context/shape mask | | 6 | Masked theme and geometry guidance | Apply all theme blends; reblend theme/old brush parameters; apply direct edits and mappings; reapply hard geometry controls and rasterize | | 7 | Prepared feature modules | Add or carve structured zones in dependency order, clipped to bounds and optional field masks | | 8 | Masked material or aggregate modifiers | Use the original captured influence to select discrete existing material IDs | | 9 | Shared network and explicit guide paths | Reserve connective space after modules/modifiers; a guide may carve Empty or paint another material | | 10 | Hard material overrides | Force the final material, including intentionally blocking a route | Schema 3 inserts accepted semantic shell/interior/aggregate proposals between steps 6 and 7 and restores explicit semantic passages after step 9. Existing native modules and material modifiers can therefore contribute to semantic places, while final hard material overrides still win. The hierarchy's final-cell route report observes that complete stack and reports any blocked passage; it does not reinterpret a hard override as optional. Recipes without grammar retain the table's preceding behavior. The [field/modifier contract](procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) defines the two guidance stages, mapping endpoints and immutable context. No earlier modifier can change the context observed by a later modifier. Recipes without new controls retain their old material behavior; fixed legacy hashes cover all three candidates in four signed chunks. Brush points are world-space `[x,y]` pairs. A single point is a dab; multiple points form a polyline. Influence uses distance to the nearest segment, a smooth radial falloff raised

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > How are themes, subsets and supersets resolved?
The recipe catalogue is a validated directed acyclic graph. A theme has an ID, zero or more parents, optional typed parameter edits, a `concrete` flag and a four-material palette. Groups expand into their concrete descendants; concrete themes are the eligible emitted palettes. A concrete theme may belong to multiple groups. Unknown parents, cycles, duplicate IDs, invalid materials and oversized catalogues are rejected before any job exists. The built-in hierarchy is: | Group | Concrete descendants | |---|---| | `natural` | `dry_cavern`, `wet_cavern`, `basalt`, `garden` | | `built` | `industrial`, `ruins`, `garden` | | `world` | All six concrete themes | `garden` intentionally belongs to both `natural` and `built`. The initial catalogue can be replaced with an explicit `catalogue` in a native recipe or Godot manifest. Palette roles are `rock`, `surface`, `accent` and `fluid`; material IDs remain discrete. Stable rock construction uses block materials, not movable `Stone`. Selection uses `themes.weights`, a mapping from group or concrete ID to a nonnegative weight. Each selected group's mass is divided equally among its eligible concrete descendants. Overlapping selections accumulate, then normalize. For example, a group containing A/B with weight 3 and an unrelated C with weight 1 resolves to A=0.375, B=0.375, C=0.25. Selecting the A/B group with weight 1 and A with weight 1 resolves to A=0.75, B=0.25. A repeated selector ID is invalid. `themes.exclude` removes an entire group or a concrete theme before normalization. Global exclusions remain hard eligibility constraints in every brush and masked theme modifier. Neither can reintroduce an excluded descendant. An all-zero or entirely excluded selection is invalid; generation never silently substitutes a fallback theme. At a cell, spatial brushes and masked theme guidance blend normalized theme weights. A uniform hash of a warped world-space patch selects a concrete palette from the effective weights. This produces coherent material regions; weights are preferences across regions, not exact material-area quotas in an arbitrary finite crop. The fallback for floating-point accumulation can only select a positive, eligible weight. Theme parameter edits inherit through parents in sorted parent order, with the child applied last. Multiple-parent conflicts therefore have explicit deterministic precedence; use a child edit to make a required value unambiguous. Palette fields belong to each concrete theme and are not implicitly inherited. Effective theme parameters blend from an eligible reference plus weighted differences, preserving identical minimum values exactly rather than rounding a one-cell wall to zero.

Section: Procedural generation fields and masked modifiers > Which context is available to guidance and sculpting?
The generator first resolves the original theme selection, old polyline brushes and hard parameter/candidate overrides, then rasterizes that initial candidate. It captures context at this point, before field-guided changes, structural modules, material/aggregate modifiers, connective carving, explicit paths or hard material overrides. All fields and modifier predicates for the cell see this same capture. | Channel | Initial proposal meaning | |---|---| | `occupied` | 1 for any non-Empty material, otherwise 0 | | `solid` | 1 only for the existing `MaterialState::Solid`; Powder is occupied but not solid | | `fluid` | 1 only for the existing `MaterialState::Liquid` | | `material` | Exact existing material ID, consumed by a `material` field or predicate | | `depth` | Downward-positive `y - surface(x)` using the original Strata surface formula | | `slope` | Absolute surface-height difference across x−1/x+1, divided by two; one-sided at the admitted coordinate boundary | | `route` | Binary initial shared-network membership for Flow Network/District Grammar; zero for Strata | The analytic surface uses the original effective `surface_y` and `relief`, even when the candidate is District Grammar. Slope recomputes the original theme, brush and hard-parameter state at each neighboring surface sample. Consequently an authored height brush can contribute slope even with zero noise relief. It does not read neighboring material occupancy or recursively evaluate fields. A modifier's `context` predicate is `any`, `empty`, `occupied`, `solid`, `fluid` or `material`; only the last requires `context_material`. For example, an occupied-only carving modifier can remove initial terrain without a later empty-only modifier treating that new hole as initially empty. Material added by a module does not retroactively change a field mask. This fixed observation point prevents order-dependent context feedback and keeps cross-chunk sampling local. The standalone graph accepts a copied `FieldContext` from a native caller. Binary channels must be finite in `[0,1]`; material IDs must exist; absolute depth and nonnegative slope are bounded by `2 * 2^40`. That value interface is not a live World-query hook. A future adapter supplying live observations would need its own immutable snapshot, revision and scheduling contract.

results.query: Do procedural aggregate definitions create new mixture physics, and does grain_size quantize a named variation field?
facts: An aggregate realizes one existing material ID per cell, with 1 through 16 unique components and strictly positive finite weights. It does not add density, reactions, fractional material state or simulation field storage.
Without a variation field, a seed-and-ID hash selects one material per signed world-aligned grain. A named variation field selects directly at each sample; grain_size does not quantize it.

Canonical recipes retain authored weights separately from prepared normalized selection. Zero, invalid IDs, duplicate components and normalization underflow reject; weights express preferences rather than finite-crop quotas.

Section: Procedural generation fields and masked modifiers > How do aggregate definitions become ordinary material cells?
An aggregate has an ID, `components`, integer `grain_size` and optional `variation` field. Each component names one existing material and a positive finite weight. The compiler accepts 1 through 16 unique materials per aggregate, rejects zero or negative weights, caps each weight at 1,000,000 and rejects normalization underflow. Remove a component to exclude it, or use the modifier's exclusion mask. These strictly positive aggregate weights differ from the existing theme-selection schema, which permits zero selectors if the overall selection is valid. Components sort by material ID. The public compiled recipe preserves authored weights; separate prepared normalized values select materials. Recompiling that canonical recipe therefore does not repeatedly renormalize weights or drift its identity. Aggregate definitions may contain powders, liquids, solids or Empty; each emitted cell remains one valid existing material ID. Without `variation`, a seed-and-ID hash selects a material for each world-aligned square grain. Floor division preserves grains across negative coordinates and output chunk boundaries. `grain_size` defaults to 4 and accepts `1..4096` cells. With `variation`, the named scalar field directly selects a component at each sample; **grain size does not quantize that field**. Values 0 and 1 select the first and last sorted components respectively. Weights are preferences rather than exact material quotas in a finite crop. Aggregate authoring introduces no new density, reaction, collision, Water, visual or save-state material schema. A generated Water cell receives ordinary native Water initialization only if the separate World owner admits its material span. The preview shows the selected material palette before simulation; it does not predict whether a mixture will settle, dissolve, flow or retain structural support.

Section: Configuration reference > Opt-in procedural generation configuration
**Current GEN-001/GEN-002 source:** [`generation::Recipe`](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) is separate from `WorldConfig` and the transport/Water profiles. Its native defaults are schema version 1, algorithm version 2, seed 1, revision 1, candidate `strata`, chunk edge 128 and the `natural` theme family. Generator chunk edges are admitted from 8 through 256 cells; complete output must remain within `-2^40 <= coordinate < 2^40`. Native World installation additionally requires its own configured chunk geometry and exclusive owner boundary. The logical operation limit defaults to 64,000,000 per chunk. Recipe capacities, numeric parameter ranges, theme inheritance, global topology controls and the different workbench starting preset belong to the [procedural generation contract](../systems/procedural-world-generation.md), with validation in [`Generator::compile`](../../native/src/world_generation.cpp). The workbench offers narrower slider ranges for some controls while its JSON editor accepts the validated native range. No general World configuration, residency or replay serialization follows from saving a generation recipe. GEN-002 optionally adds up to 64 fields, 32 aggregates and 64 modifiers. The scalar graph caps depth at 16 and declared operations at 4096 per sample. Aggregates admit 1..16 unique existing material IDs with strictly positive finite weights; their grain size defaults to 4 and accepts integers 1..4096. Named variation fields select per cell without grain quantization. Field defaults/arity/ranges are exposed by native `field_kind_specs()` and copied by `get_catalogue`. The [field/modifier contract](../systems/procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) owns these values, context meaning, masks and diagnostic bounds; these scalar authoring fields do not allocate optional simulation temperature/pressure storage. **Current GEN-003 opt-in schema 2:** the separate typed `spatial` graph uses generator algorithm 3 and spatial algorithm 1. Schema 1 retains the preceding algorithm and scalar contracts. `spatial_limits` defaults to 64 expanded nodes, dependency depth 16, 1,000,000 logical operations per sample, 16,000,000 preparation operations and 16 MiB preparation storage. Nodes declare scales 1/4/16/64 cells; sampling uses a fixed 256-entry caller-owned cache. Subgraphs/instances have bounded expansion and parameter counts; recursive definitions are rejected. Internal resampling admits the bounded ±`2^44` footprint while public cells remain in `[-2^40,2^40)`. Continuous component bounds stay within ±`1e100`; unit exponents stay within −8..8. Derivative spacing is 1..64 cells and warp displacement 0..4096 cells. Exact category IDs retain integer components. Geometry has at most 256 points. Region assignment has at most 16×16 cells and 16 categories, a default 1,000,000-operation preparation budget, hard work ceiling 64,000,000 and fixed bounded solver scratch. Repeated tiles require explicit wrap constraints for cross-tile adjacency guarantees. The [typed contract](../systems/procedural-typed-spatial-fields.md) and [operator inventory](procedural-spatial-operators.md) own exact family ranges, recursive cost composition, distance qualification and invalid-input behavior.

Section: Procedural generation fields and masked modifiers > What do Hilbert and Morton guarantee at signed chunk boundaries?
Curve tiles have side `2^order`, where `order` is an integer from 1 through 20. Each local curve cell covers `cell_size` world cells per axis, an integer from 1 through 4096. Origin coordinates are integer cells. At the maximum settings, one tile spans `2^32` world cells per axis; intermediate address arithmetic is wide enough for that extent. `curve_address(kind, x, y, order, cell_size, origin_x, origin_y)` returns signed tile coordinates, local unsigned coordinates and a local rank. Floor division assigns negative cells consistently. `curve_index` and `curve_point` convert between local coordinates and rank without sampling any neighbor. Scalar curve fields divide the rank by `2^(2*order)-1`, retaining exact endpoint values. Hilbert order 1 visits `(0,0)`, `(0,1)`, `(1,1)`, `(1,0)`. Consecutive Hilbert ranks share an edge **within the same finite tile**. Tiling repeats that local addressing pattern; there is no promised continuous infinite Hilbert path between tiles. Morton interleaves x bits in even lanes and y bits in odd lanes; successive Morton ranks need not share an edge. A Morton field is therefore a spatial ordering control, not an automatically connected corridor. The generator's separately defined macrocell hub/port network owns interconnected routes. Curve fields may guide material seams, masks, variation or parameter mapping without replacing that connectivity contract. Both curve ranks and resulting material proposals stay independent of output chunk size, including partitions and brush shapes crossing negative coordinates. Samples must lie inside `[-2^40,2^40)`; curve and field origin parameters accept both endpoints of `[-2^40,2^40]`. Out-of-domain requests and invalid curve ranks, local coordinates, orders or cell sizes reject explicitly.

results.query: Does hiding a generator modifier or selecting a diagnostic bypass budgets, and can an old inspection packet enter a new preview or live World?
facts: The field graph caps 64 declarations, depth 16 and 4096 logical operations per sample. All declared field/modifier/component/module work counts even when masked; zero module influence avoids its callback but not its declared charge.

A field, modifier or module diagnostic is collected as normalized floats during paced cell generation. Its channel, shape and float bits join the receipt; altered data reject, and failure or cancellation discards both materials and diagnostics.

The workbench validates recipe identity, expected coordinate, inspection token, channel and values before caching copied proposals. It has no live World installer; native admission still requires current recipe acceptance and caller-owned World/reset lifetime.

Section: Data ownership and lifetimes > How may generated content enter cell authority?
**Current GEN-001/GEN-002 source:** the generation job API and supplied module context provide no mutable World, scene-tree or Rapier state. The [generation contract](../systems/procedural-world-generation.md) separates immutable recipe/revision receipts from the destination World's lifetime. `Generator::accepts` validates the former; the caller must also establish the current World/reset session and hold exclusive ownership before invoking [`World::install_generated_chunk`](../../native/src/world.cpp). Installation prevalidates one complete material span before allocating/writing, requires an absent destination chunk and uses existing native mutation defaults. Even a reserved empty or edited-then-cleared resident chunk is protected from regeneration. Failed Worlds, in-tick calls, invalid payloads, capacity/coordinate failure and overlapping transient occupancy are explicit refusals. This method is a loading/setup boundary primitive; it supplies no background World owner, automatic resident eviction or reset-session manager. The opt-in workbench only previews copied proposals and never calls it on the sandbox World. GEN-002 scalar context observes the initial procedural candidate, including its old brushes and hard geometry controls, before any masked modifier or module. It does not borrow live World material or infer player edits from empty preview cells. Diagnostic floats are job-owned and receipt-bound, then copied into the workbench cache; changing inspection channels retires that cache. The [field/modifier contract](../systems/procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) owns this immutable-context and diagnostic lifecycle. GEN-003 schema-2 [`SpatialGraph`](../../native/include/cybersand/generation_typed_fields.hpp) adds immutable typed functions beside that retained context graph. It never resamples `FieldContext` as if it contained neighboring observations. Route and feature geometry is copied; finite region assignments finish preparation before publication. Each caller or job owns its bounded sampling scratch. Typed diagnostics preserve signed values, vector components and exact categorical identities; the chunk receipt binds both payload and type/unit metadata, and failure/cancellation publishes neither materials nor diagnostics. The [typed contract](../systems/procedural-typed-spatial-fields.md) owns these lifetimes and cache identities. Future grammar, authoring and streaming owners may consume the interfaces without gaining mutable cell access.

Section: Interfaces and message contracts > Current public surfaces > Native procedural generation and fresh-chunk admission
**Current GEN-001/GEN-002 source:** [`generation::Generator`](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) compiles a value-only recipe into immutable theme/field/aggregate/module state. `begin(ChunkCoord, diagnostic="")` creates a private `GenerationJob`; `advance(cell_budget)` limits work, and `result()` refuses access while pending. Ready results contain copied row-major materials, coordinates, revision, recipe fingerprint, content hash and an admission receipt binding those identities and optional diagnostic channel/float data. Failed/cancelled jobs expose neither cell nor diagnostic payload. `accepts(result)` checks complete current recipe/receipt identity; it does not identify the lifetime of a separate mutable World. [`World::install_generated_chunk`](../../native/src/world.cpp) takes a coordinate and immutable material span under the existing exclusive owner, between ticks. It validates the whole payload and admits only an absent storage chunk; resident empty, reserved and edited-then-cleared chunks remain protected. Its explicit outcomes cover refusal/capacity/ownership conditions. Section: Procedural generation fields and masked modifiers > How are diagnostics, budgets and lifetimes bounded?
`Generator::begin(chunk, diagnostic)` and synchronous `generate` accept an empty channel or exactly one of `field:<id>`, `modifier:<id>` and `module:<id>`. These report the scalar output, effective modifier influence or bounded module mask. Unknown channels reject before job preparation. A requested diagnostic allocates one float per cell beside the private material array and is filled during normal paced generation, not a second generation pass. Ready `ChunkResult` values contain the channel name and optional normalized `float` diagnostics. The material content hash is unchanged by inspection; the receipt binds channel name, shape and float bit patterns as well as material, coordinate and recipe identity. `accepts` rejects altered, missing, nonfinite or out-of-range diagnostic data. Failure and cancellation discard both material and diagnostic payloads and their hashes. Pending prefixes remain private. | Bound | Current default / hard ceiling | |---|---| | Field declarations | 64 | | Field dependency depth | 16, including warp references | | Scalar logical work | 4096 operations per sample | | Aggregate definitions | 32, each with 1..16 components | | Modifiers | 64; existing point and geometry bounds also apply | | Material chunk | Side 8..256; at most 65,536 material bytes | | Requested diagnostic | At most 65,536 float values / 262,144 payload bytes | | Chunk logical work | Default 64,000,000; diagnostic adds four operations per cell | All field nodes, configured modifier work, aggregate components and declared module costs count toward logical work even when an application mask is zero. The integrated charge includes immutable-context construction, the two surface parameter snapshots used for slope and guided rerasterization. Limits bound declared work; they are not measured CPU instructions, wall-time deadlines or a sandbox for arbitrary registered C++ callbacks. Excess work fails and publishes no partial payload. Jobs retain an immutable compiled generator and prepared field/module state. Changing a recipe cannot mutate a prior job. This retained schema-1 path uses generator algorithm version 2 and scalar field algorithm version 1. Explicit schema-2 recipes use generator algorithm 3 and the separate spatial algorithm 1; their type-aware receipts and diagnostics follow the [typed contract](procedural-typed-spatial-fields.md). Twelve independently retained GEN-001 material hashes cover three candidates in four signed chunks with the old complex controls and no new fields/modifiers. Those regressions protect the measured legacy material output; algorithm identity and receipts intentionally change with the new implementation version.
