Section: Procedural world generation candidates > How do chunks connect without generating neighbors?
Every field is sampled at global coordinates. Seeded lattice values depend on seed, coordinates and an algorithm lane, not a mutable PRNG sequence. Changing request order, slicing a job into different cell budgets, or partitioning the same region into different chunk sizes therefore leaves its material cells unchanged for the same effective recipe. Flow Network and District Grammar divide the plane into fixed macrocells. Each cell has a seeded interior hub. An edge's port is derived from a canonical edge coordinate and axis; its two owners independently obtain the same port. Each hub connects to all four edge ports. No recursive neighbor request, global graph construction, speculative edge negotiation or neighbor-residency check is needed. The shared skeleton is carved after feature modules and material modifiers so their ordinary walls do not seal it. An independent regression fills the region with solid Metal and requires a four-neighbor Empty component across a negative-coordinate 2x2 macrocell region to reach every outer side. The current guarantee is a deterministic raster connection in one unchanged recipe. It does not guarantee that independently edited recipes meet, that a large player fits every passage, or that a passage containing later simulation material remains traversable. Explicit hard material/candidate changes may alter connectivity by design. The workbench replaces its complete preview revision after an edit, avoiding a mixture of old and new generated chunks. Native World supports wider signed coordinates. This generator deliberately accepts only complete chunks inside `[-2^40,2^40)` cell coordinates: brush geometry uses doubles, and out-of-domain requests must refuse rather than alias distant positions. Negative coordinates use mathematical floor division. A job must fit the entire chunk in that domain before allocating its output.

results.query: Does the Peano spatial traversal make an infinite connected route, and how are Voronoi ties and Delaunay co-circular diagonals handled?
facts: Peano covers a finite 3^order square with order 1..12; its rank/inverse are bijective and successive ranks share an edge only inside that tile.
Repeated finite traversal does not imply connected physical routes between tiles.
Voronoi has one deterministically jittered seed per world lattice tile, a fixed 5x5 nearest search and lexicographic signed-coordinate ties.
Delaunay-derived adjacency is the positive-length Voronoi-face dual; zero-length co-circular diagonal edges are omitted.

Section: Typed spatial fields, transforms and reusable generation graphs > What do Peano, Voronoi, Delaunay and Poisson guarantee?
The Peano operator extends the retained finite Hilbert/Morton controls with a ternary square traversal. Side length is `3^order`, `order=1..12`; each local cell spans `cell_size=1..4096` world cells. Rank and inverse are bijections. Consecutive Peano ranks share an edge **inside one finite tile**. Signed tile addressing uses floor division. No infinite path or physical route is promised between independently repeated tiles; authored routes and the generator's shared-network controls retain that separate role. Voronoi seeds use one deterministically jittered point in each world-aligned lattice tile. `spacing` is `1..1,048,576` cells and `jitter` is `[0,1]`. A fixed 5×5 candidate search suffices for the nearest point because the containing tile always supplies a seed within `sqrt(2)*spacing`. Equal distances choose the lexicographically smaller signed seed coordinate. Region identity retains both seed coordinates and a stable graph domain; it does not pack an unbounded address into a floating-point number. `voronoi_distance` returns nearest-seed distance. `voronoi_boundary` measures distance to the nearest competing Voronoi boundary under its bounded 7×7 competitor search. `delaunay_degree` exposes the size of the positive-length Voronoi-face dual. The lower-level neighborhood API additionally returns incident neighbors/positions and distance to the owner's incident segments. Co-circular zero-length diagonal edges are deliberately omitted; a square lattice therefore has four face neighbors rather than an arbitrary triangulation diagonal. This is the documented Delaunay-derived structure. Poisson-style seeds use deterministic Matérn-II priority rejection. Each lattice tile owns one candidate. It survives only if no candidate within the authored radius has a lower `(priority, signed ID)` ordering. Rejected candidates still compete; acceptance never recursively asks whether a neighbor survived. Radius must be positive and no greater than twice the lattice spacing. Candidate ownership is half-open and independent of requested chunks. The query radius is `R=search_cells*spacing`, with `search_cells=1..4`. `poisson_found` reports whether an accepted seed lies strictly inside R. `poisson_distance` returns the nearest accepted distance capped at R. A `poisson_region` identity must be interpreted together with `poisson_found` when no candidate is found. This bounded selection gives hard minimum separation, not a guaranteed globally nearest seed, maximal packing or a measured blue-noise spectral guarantee.

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > What is implemented?
**Current candidate source, GEN-001 / [#163](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/163) and GEN-002 / [#171](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/171):** three CPU procedural generators share one immutable recipe, theme hierarchy, spatial control stack and extensible native feature registry. They produce actual material IDs for signed-coordinate chunks. Generation is separate from simulation: it does not tick materials, query a mutable World, call Godot, request neighboring chunks or share a mutable random generator. The [public native API](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) and [implementation](../../native/src/world_generation.cpp) own these semantics. GEN-002 adds named structured-noise/finite-curve fields, scalar sidechains, masked context-aware guidance and sculpting, aggregate material recipes and paced diagnostic channels. The focused [fields and modifiers contract](procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) owns those controls, immutable initial context and finite Hilbert/Morton scope. GEN-003 / [#190](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/190) adds explicit schema-2 [typed spatial functions](procedural-typed-spatial-fields.md): signed distance/vector/category values, transformed/derived geometry, reusable parameter subgraphs, structured seeds, finite adjacency assignments and world-aligned multiresolution sampling. The retained scalar graph remains separately defined; typed spatial functions have no per-cell initial-context input. Only explicit normalized `spatial:<id>` outputs may drive existing masks and mappings. GEN-004 / [#191](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/191) adds explicit schema-3 [hierarchical semantic plans](procedural-hierarchical-generation.md). Finite canonical regions own nested places and cross-chunk structures; stable rule/slot IDs, placement constraints, matched sockets, explicit loops/service trunks and final-raster route reports precede ordinary chunk publication. Selected immutable semantic geometries may feed the typed graph. The hierarchy does not add World streaming or replace final hard material authority. | Candidate | Generated structure | Suitable starting point | |---|---|---| | `strata` | Smoothly varying surface, domain-warped caves, strata, deposits and material-specific deep fill | Organic terrain, underground spaces and theme transitions | | `flow_network` | Strata plus a connected macrocell hub/port network, carved after structural modules | Interconnected passages, service routes and excavation networks | | `district_grammar` | Global room/floor lattice with repeated doors and accents, plus the same hub/port network | Dense urban interiors, industrial districts and structured construction | ![Actual native generation with the same authored controls across the three candidates](../figures/worldgen-candidates.png) Seed 314159; each panel covers 512 by 384 cells at origin `[-256,0]`. Reproduce the material pixels with `make worldgen-demo`. This is generation output, before simulation. Every candidate consumes the same brushes, paths, overrides and feature instances. A hard candidate override can choose another generator inside a rectangular zone. This is deliberately a set of provisional algorithms, not a selected production world style or a proof of useful player navigation. In particular, generator connectivity does not establish actor clearance, gravity traversal or fluid equilibrium; the existing material and actor owners retain those semantics. **Current authoring surface:** the separate [worldgen workbench](../../godot/worldgen_workbench.tscn) previews generated material pixels and performs bounded demand generation while panning.

This does not promise maximal packing, a globally nearest seed outside the search radius or a measured blue-noise spectral property.

Section: Configuration reference > Opt-in procedural generation configuration
**Current GEN-001/GEN-002 source:** [`generation::Recipe`](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) is separate from `WorldConfig` and the transport/Water profiles. Its native defaults are schema version 1, algorithm version 2, seed 1, revision 1, candidate `strata`, chunk edge 128 and the `natural` theme family. Generator chunk edges are admitted from 8 through 256 cells; complete output must remain within `-2^40 <= coordinate < 2^40`. Native World installation additionally requires its own configured chunk geometry and exclusive owner boundary. The logical operation limit defaults to 64,000,000 per chunk. Recipe capacities, numeric parameter ranges, theme inheritance, global topology controls and the different workbench starting preset belong to the [procedural generation contract](../systems/procedural-world-generation.md), with validation in [`Generator::compile`](../../native/src/world_generation.cpp). The workbench offers narrower slider ranges for some controls while its JSON editor accepts the validated native range. No general World configuration, residency or replay serialization follows from saving a generation recipe. GEN-002 optionally adds up to 64 fields, 32 aggregates and 64 modifiers. The scalar graph caps depth at 16 and declared operations at 4096 per sample. Aggregates admit 1..16 unique existing material IDs with strictly positive finite weights; their grain size defaults to 4 and accepts integers 1..4096. Named variation fields select per cell without grain quantization. Field defaults/arity/ranges are exposed by native `field_kind_specs()` and copied by `get_catalogue`. The [field/modifier contract](../systems/procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) owns these values, context meaning, masks and diagnostic bounds; these scalar authoring fields do not allocate optional simulation temperature/pressure storage. **Current GEN-003 opt-in schema 2:** the separate typed `spatial` graph uses generator algorithm 3 and spatial algorithm 1. Schema 1 retains the preceding algorithm and scalar contracts. `spatial_limits` defaults to 64 expanded nodes, dependency depth 16, 1,000,000 logical operations per sample, 16,000,000 preparation operations and 16 MiB preparation storage. Nodes declare scales 1/4/16/64 cells; sampling uses a fixed 256-entry caller-owned cache. Subgraphs/instances have bounded expansion and parameter counts; recursive definitions are rejected. Internal resampling admits the bounded ±`2^44` footprint while public cells remain in `[-2^40,2^40)`. Continuous component bounds stay within ±`1e100`; unit exponents stay within −8..8. Derivative spacing is 1..64 cells and warp displacement 0..4096 cells. Exact category IDs retain integer components. Geometry has at most 256 points. Region assignment has at most 16×16 cells and 16 categories, a default 1,000,000-operation preparation budget, hard work ceiling 64,000,000 and fixed bounded solver scratch. Repeated tiles require explicit wrap constraints for cross-tile adjacency guarantees. The [typed contract](../systems/procedural-typed-spatial-fields.md) and [operator inventory](procedural-spatial-operators.md) own exact family ranges, recursive cost composition, distance qualification and invalid-input behavior.

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > What is implemented?
**Current candidate source, GEN-001 / [#163](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/163) and GEN-002 / [#171](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/171):** three CPU procedural generators share one immutable recipe, theme hierarchy, spatial control stack and extensible native feature registry. They produce actual material IDs for signed-coordinate chunks. Generation is separate from simulation: it does not tick materials, query a mutable World, call Godot, request neighboring chunks or share a mutable random generator. The [public native API](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) and [implementation](../../native/src/world_generation.cpp) own these semantics. GEN-002 adds named structured-noise/finite-curve fields, scalar sidechains, masked context-aware guidance and sculpting, aggregate material recipes and paced diagnostic channels. The focused [fields and modifiers contract](procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) owns those controls, immutable initial context and finite Hilbert/Morton scope. GEN-003 / [#190](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/190) adds explicit schema-2 [typed spatial functions](procedural-typed-spatial-fields.md): signed distance/vector/category values, transformed/derived geometry, reusable parameter subgraphs, structured seeds, finite adjacency assignments and world-aligned multiresolution sampling. The retained scalar graph remains separately defined; typed spatial functions have no per-cell initial-context input. Only explicit normalized `spatial:<id>` outputs may drive existing masks and mappings. GEN-004 / [#191](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/191) adds explicit schema-3 [hierarchical semantic plans](procedural-hierarchical-generation.md). Finite canonical regions own nested places and cross-chunk structures; stable rule/slot IDs, placement constraints, matched sockets, explicit loops/service trunks and final-raster route reports precede ordinary chunk publication. Selected immutable semantic geometries may feed the typed graph. The hierarchy does not add World streaming or replace final hard material authority. | Candidate | Generated structure | Suitable starting point | |---|---|---| | `strata` | Smoothly varying surface, domain-warped caves, strata, deposits and material-specific deep fill | Organic terrain, underground spaces and theme transitions | | `flow_network` | Strata plus a connected macrocell hub/port network, carved after structural modules | Interconnected passages, service routes and excavation networks | | `district_grammar` | Global room/floor lattice with repeated doors and accents, plus the same hub/port network | Dense urban interiors, industrial districts and structured construction | ![Actual native generation with the same authored controls across the three candidates](../figures/worldgen-candidates.png) Seed 314159; each panel covers 512 by 384 cells at origin `[-256,0]`. Reproduce the material pixels with `make worldgen-demo`. This is generation output, before simulation. Every candidate consumes the same brushes, paths, overrides and feature instances. A hard candidate override can choose another generator inside a rectangular zone. This is deliberately a set of provisional algorithms, not a selected production world style or a proof of useful player navigation. In particular, generator connectivity does not establish actor clearance, gravity traversal or fluid equilibrium; the existing material and actor owners retain those semantics. **Current authoring surface:** the separate [worldgen workbench](../../godot/worldgen_workbench.tscn) previews generated material pixels and performs bounded demand generation while panning.

Geometry inputs contain an ID, 1..256 finite points and a `closed` flag; a closed boundary requires at least three points. `geometry_distance` names one immutable input and returns Euclidean distance to its point, open polyline segments or closed boundary. Closed geometry measures the boundary; it does not silently become an inside/outside classifier. A single point and repeated points have bounded explicit segment handling. Geometry is copied/prepared before publication, and its actual coordinates enter the consuming node's identity. GEN-004 can supply routes and feature boundaries through this value interface without a dependency from fields into the future grammar implementation. An assignment input declares a finite tile of at most 16×16 cells, up to 16 exact categories, four directional adjacency masks and optional per-cell domain masks. Opposite adjacency relations must be reciprocal. Deterministic propagation and bounded backtracking prepare the entire solution before a field can sample it. Unsatisfiable constraints and exhausted work are distinct explicit failures; neither exposes a partial assignment. `assigned_region` returns one exact category from the prepared tile. The tile repeats using floor addressing. `wrap_x`/`wrap_y` enable constraints across those tile edges; without a wrap constraint, adjacency is guaranteed only inside the finite tile. GEN-004 owns hierarchical layout use of this contract and should reuse this solver rather than introducing a conflicting field solver.

Section: Typed spatial fields, transforms and reusable generation graphs > What do Peano, Voronoi, Delaunay and Poisson guarantee?
The Peano operator extends the retained finite Hilbert/Morton controls with a ternary square traversal. Side length is `3^order`, `order=1..12`; each local cell spans `cell_size=1..4096` world cells. Rank and inverse are bijections. Consecutive Peano ranks share an edge **inside one finite tile**. Signed tile addressing uses floor division. No infinite path or physical route is promised between independently repeated tiles; authored routes and the generator's shared-network controls retain that separate role. Voronoi seeds use one deterministically jittered point in each world-aligned lattice tile. `spacing` is `1..1,048,576` cells and `jitter` is `[0,1]`. A fixed 5×5 candidate search suffices for the nearest point because the containing tile always supplies a seed within `sqrt(2)*spacing`. Equal distances choose the lexicographically smaller signed seed coordinate. Region identity retains both seed coordinates and a stable graph domain; it does not pack an unbounded address into a floating-point number. `voronoi_distance` returns nearest-seed distance. `voronoi_boundary` measures distance to the nearest competing Voronoi boundary under its bounded 7×7 competitor search. `delaunay_degree` exposes the size of the positive-length Voronoi-face dual. The lower-level neighborhood API additionally returns incident neighbors/positions and distance to the owner's incident segments. Co-circular zero-length diagonal edges are deliberately omitted; a square lattice therefore has four face neighbors rather than an arbitrary triangulation diagonal. This is the documented Delaunay-derived structure. Poisson-style seeds use deterministic Matérn-II priority rejection. Each lattice tile owns one candidate. It survives only if no candidate within the authored radius has a lower `(priority, signed ID)` ordering. Rejected candidates still compete; acceptance never recursively asks whether a neighbor survived. Radius must be positive and no greater than twice the lattice spacing. Candidate ownership is half-open and independent of requested chunks. The query radius is `R=search_cells*spacing`, with `search_cells=1..4`. `poisson_found` reports whether an accepted seed lies strictly inside R. `poisson_distance` returns the nearest accepted distance capped at R. A `poisson_region` identity must be interpreted together with `poisson_found` when no candidate is found. This bounded selection gives hard minimum separation, not a guaranteed globally nearest seed, maximal packing or a measured blue-noise spectral guarantee.

GEN-004 compiles immutable semantic plans in a finite, authored window of world-zero-anchored regions. Section: Typed spatial fields, transforms and reusable generation graphs > How do multiresolution evaluation, caches and budgets behave?
Every node declares `sampling_scale` of 1, 4, 16 or 64 cells. The lattice is anchored at absolute world zero using mathematical floor, including negative positions. Continuous outputs use deterministic bilinear interpolation between the four coarse anchors. Categorical and boolean outputs select the nearest anchor exactly; an exact half tie selects the lower anchor on each axis. IDs and booleans are never numerically interpolated. Coarse distance interpolation loses exact-distance qualification. The caller-owned `SpatialScratch` contains 256 bounded cache entries. Keys bind the transitive node identity, exact double coordinate bits and sampling mode; the graph contains no mutable cache. Identity includes algorithm, operator, parameters, instance path/seed, inputs, referenced geometry/assignment and sampling scale. Warm, cold or evicted entries change work reuse, not results. Separate workers use separate scratch. In particular, no cache key needs a live World revision because the typed API has no World or per-cell context access. Numeric negative zero is canonicalized to positive zero in both identity and returned components, so sharing cached results between equivalent definitions cannot change their component bits. The numerical implementation uses ordinary C++ double arithmetic and standard transcendental functions. Exact equality is the supported deterministic guarantee for the same compiled numerical implementation under different request order, partitions, worker scratches, budget slices and cache states. Cross-platform bitwise equivalence of trigonometry/logarithms is not promised by this contract; Linux and Windows execution remain individually source-bound acceptance gates. The compiler accounts for recursive source sampling, derivative fan-out, coarse four-anchor sampling, every expanded declaration, seed neighborhoods, geometry segments and solver preparation. Declared work is conservative logical work, not wall-clock time or exact machine instructions; cache hits do not reduce the admission charge. Bounds and defaults are in the [configuration reference](../reference/configuration-reference.md#opt-in-procedural-generation-configuration). Successful evaluation uses fixed caller/stack scratch without per-cell heap growth. `evaluate` fills a private result before replacing the caller's output. Generation retains its private pending material/diagnostic arrays; cancellation or failure discards both payloads and their receipt hashes. A ready chunk is one complete result. Compilation, preparation and per-chunk rejection are not permission to expose a partially generated map.

Section: Typed spatial fields, transforms and reusable generation graphs > How are named subgraphs and parameters expanded?
A `spatial` definition contains `nodes`, `subgraphs`, `instances`, `geometries` and `assignments`. A named subgraph declares typed parameters with optional defaults, local nodes, nested instances and named outputs. Instances supply typed literal `bindings`; nested instances may bind parameters from their enclosing subgraph. Numeric operator parameters can explicitly refer to a typed scalar parameter through `parameter_bindings`. The declared cell exponent must match the operator parameter: lengths, positions and sampling spacing use one; angles, affine scale factors, shears, jitter, salt and traversal order use zero. `to_mask` low/high bounds inherit the input field's exponent. Numeric bindings are not an escape from unit checking. A `parameter` node names its declaration with `reference` and may select a sampling scale; its type, units and value come from the declaration/binding, so ignored node-level overrides reject. Local IDs allow letters, digits, hyphen and underscore. Dot is reserved for expanded namespaces. An output named `mask` in instance `decay` is `decay.mask`; a nested instance adds another namespace component. The compiler rejects duplicate IDs, node/instance/output collisions, unknown bindings, missing required inputs, wrong types, dependency cycles and recursive expansion. Unused declarations are validated too. Root graph nodes may consume an expanded output by its full name. The definition admits at most 16 subgraphs, root instances, geometry inputs and assignments per family. Each subgraph admits at most 16 parameters, nested instances and named outputs; nesting depth is at most eight. Expansion shares a hard 1,024-instance-call ledger across actual and unused-template validation, so even a tree of empty subgraphs has bounded work. Every expansion call costs 512 preparation units and every expanded node costs 8,192, in addition to declaration validation and geometry/solver preparation. Stable instance paths derive deterministic seed domains from the recipe seed. Reordering declaration arrays does not alter meaning. A parameter edit changes the consuming node and its transitive consumers; unrelated instance/node identities remain reusable. Compiled inputs are immutable owned values, so editing the author's definition cannot mutate a retained graph or pending job.

Section: Typed spatial fields, transforms and reusable generation graphs > How are coordinate transforms composed?
`transform` samples its source in local coordinates. For local point `q`, world point `p`, origin `o`, translation `t`, rotation `R`, shear `H` and anisotropic scale `S`, the convention is: ```text p = o + t + R H S (q − o) q = o + (R H S)^−1 (p − o − t) H = [[1, shear_x], [shear_y, 1]] S = diag(sx, sy) ``` Positive angles use the ordinary coordinate rotation matrix. World y is the generator's downward-positive axis, so the on-screen visual interpretation follows that axis convention. Translation and origin are positions in cells; angles are radians. Nested transforms compose through explicit source inputs and are bounded by graph depth and recursive sampling work. `transform_vector` samples its vector source at the original point and applies the **forward linear part** `R H S`. It does not add translation or origin. Coordinate deformation of a vector field and transformation of its vector values are therefore separate operations an author may compose deliberately. The compiler rejects zero/tiny scales, singular shears, nonfinite parameters and excessive declared bounds. Translation, rotation/reflection and uniform scale preserve an exact SDF. A uniform scale multiplies the sampled distance by the absolute scale. Anisotropic scaling or shear preserves the zero set but changes the result to a general implicit scalar. Its reported minimum/maximum distance factors are the affine matrix's singular-value bounds: multiplying the absolute local distance by those factors bounds the world distance to the transformed boundary. General warps, polar maps and coarse interpolation discard an exact-distance claim. Do not use a warped scalar as an exact clearance radius. `repeat` subtracts its phase origin and maps each axis into local `[0,period)` using floor-equivalent remainder. `mirror` folds the phase-shifted, period-doubled axis into local `[0,period]`. Negative inputs and exact seams obey the same rules as positive inputs. These coordinate maps repeat a function; they do not imply that material routes connect across the repeated boundary. `polar` samples its source at `(radius/radial_scale, angle/angular_scale)`; `log_polar` replaces the first component with `log(max(radius,min_radius)/radial_scale)`. Both measure radius/angle relative to an explicit origin. Angle uses `atan2`, with angle zero at the origin; the negative-x, zero-y branch is positive pi. Radial/angular scales map physical radius/radians into the source's sampling coordinates. The logarithm's minimum-radius clamp and angle branch seam are explicit numerical conventions, independent of resident chunks. `warp` takes `[source, displacement_vector]`; the displacement is sampled at the original point and radially capped to `max_displacement` cells before resampling the source. Repeated composition is bounded; no neighbor-generation recursion is introduced. Public samples use integer world coordinates in `[-2^40,2^40)`. Internal transformed,

Section: Typed spatial fields, transforms and reusable generation graphs > How do multiresolution evaluation, caches and budgets behave?
Every node declares `sampling_scale` of 1, 4, 16 or 64 cells. The lattice is anchored at absolute world zero using mathematical floor, including negative positions. Continuous outputs use deterministic bilinear interpolation between the four coarse anchors. Categorical and boolean outputs select the nearest anchor exactly; an exact half tie selects the lower anchor on each axis. IDs and booleans are never numerically interpolated. Coarse distance interpolation loses exact-distance qualification. The caller-owned `SpatialScratch` contains 256 bounded cache entries. Keys bind the transitive node identity, exact double coordinate bits and sampling mode; the graph contains no mutable cache. Identity includes algorithm, operator, parameters, instance path/seed, inputs, referenced geometry/assignment and sampling scale. Warm, cold or evicted entries change work reuse, not results. Separate workers use separate scratch. In particular, no cache key needs a live World revision because the typed API has no World or per-cell context access. Numeric negative zero is canonicalized to positive zero in both identity and returned components, so sharing cached results between equivalent definitions cannot change their component bits. The numerical implementation uses ordinary C++ double arithmetic and standard transcendental functions. Exact equality is the supported deterministic guarantee for the same compiled numerical implementation under different request order, partitions, worker scratches, budget slices and cache states. Cross-platform bitwise equivalence of trigonometry/logarithms is not promised by this contract; Linux and Windows execution remain individually source-bound acceptance gates. The compiler accounts for recursive source sampling, derivative fan-out, coarse four-anchor sampling, every expanded declaration, seed neighborhoods, geometry segments and solver preparation. Declared work is conservative logical work, not wall-clock time or exact machine instructions; cache hits do not reduce the admission charge. Bounds and defaults are in the [configuration reference](../reference/configuration-reference.md#opt-in-procedural-generation-configuration). Successful evaluation uses fixed caller/stack scratch without per-cell heap growth. `evaluate` fills a private result before replacing the caller's output. Generation retains its private pending material/diagnostic arrays; cancellation or failure discards both payloads and their receipt hashes. A ready chunk is one complete result. Compilation, preparation and per-chunk rejection are not permission to expose a partially generated map.

Generator chunk edges are admitted from 8 through 256 cells; complete output must remain within `-2^40 <= coordinate < 2^40`. Native World installation additionally requires its own configured chunk geometry and exclusive owner boundary. The logical operation limit defaults to 64,000,000 per chunk. Recipe capacities, numeric parameter ranges, theme inheritance, global topology controls and the different workbench starting preset belong to the [procedural generation contract](../systems/procedural-world-generation.md), with validation in [`Generator::compile`](../../native/src/world_generation.cpp). The workbench offers narrower slider ranges for some controls while its JSON editor accepts the validated native range. No general World configuration, residency or replay serialization follows from saving a generation recipe. GEN-002 optionally adds up to 64 fields, 32 aggregates and 64 modifiers. The scalar graph caps depth at 16 and declared operations at 4096 per sample. Aggregates admit 1..16 unique existing material IDs with strictly positive finite weights; their grain size defaults to 4 and accepts integers 1..4096. Named variation fields select per cell without grain quantization. Field defaults/arity/ranges are exposed by native `field_kind_specs()` and copied by `get_catalogue`. The [field/modifier contract](../systems/procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) owns these values, context meaning, masks and diagnostic bounds; these scalar authoring fields do not allocate optional simulation temperature/pressure storage. **Current GEN-003 opt-in schema 2:** the separate typed `spatial` graph uses generator algorithm 3 and spatial algorithm 1. Derivative spacing is 1..64 cells and warp displacement 0..4096 cells. Exact category IDs retain integer components. Geometry has at most 256 points. Region assignment has at most 16×16 cells and 16 categories, a default 1,000,000-operation preparation budget, hard work ceiling 64,000,000 and fixed bounded solver scratch. Repeated tiles require explicit wrap constraints for cross-tile adjacency guarantees. Section: Typed spatial fields, transforms and reusable generation graphs > Which values and units are preserved?
Every output has a declared type, cell-unit exponent, component bounds, natural sampling scale, identity and conservative work cost. Unit exponents range from −8 through 8. Coordinates and geometric distances have `cells^1`; gradients reduce the input exponent by one; products add exponents. Angles are radians with exponent zero. All numeric values are finite and bounded by the declared component range within ±`1e100`. | Type | Meaning | Conversion and comparison | |---|---|---| | `normalized` | Dimensionless scalar in `[0,1]` | May drive a material mask directly through a `spatial:<id>` reference | | `scalar` | General scalar, including signed values, with a declared unit exponent | No implicit clamping; `to_mask` explicitly maps its `low..high` interval into `[0,1]` | | `signed_distance` | Negative inside, zero at the boundary, positive outside, measured in cells | Only supported exact constructions retain this qualification; arbitrary arithmetic loses it | | `distance` | Nonnegative distance to a declared feature, with the operator's stated search scope | Bounded Poisson distance is a capped local search result; it is not an infinite-world nearest-seed guarantee | | `vector2` | Two continuous components sharing one unit exponent | Vector arithmetic, components, length, dot and normalization are explicit | | `category` | Exact tuple of signed integer x/y identity plus a 64-bit domain | Equality compares the full tuple; IDs are never numerically blended or converted to a mask | | `boolean` | Exact false/true, represented by zero/one | `equal`, `less` and local extrema produce it; explicit `to_mask` yields exact zero/one | Addition/subtraction and ordered scalar comparison require compatible units. Vector components require equal units. `equal` requires matching types and units, including exact categorical tuples. `select` consumes `[boolean, true_value, false_value]` with matching branch types/units. `mix` requires matching continuous inputs and a normalized weight. No categorical ordering or arithmetic is inferred from its payload. `category_is` compares a categorical input with an exact authored tuple. Its explicit literal domain zero selects the signed x/y ID within the input's own domain; a nonzero literal also requires exact domain equality. This supplies a declarative selector for generated district identities without requiring an author to reproduce the compiler's domain fingerprint. Ordinary `equal` still compares complete tuples. `constant` accepts normalized, general scalar, vector, category or boolean values. A constant with cell units is not automatically a distance to a shape. Distance types come from declared geometric operators. In JSON, categorical integers use exact text representations: signed decimal strings for x/y and exactly 16 lowercase hexadecimal digits for the unsigned domain. Section: Procedural spatial operator inventory > Interpolation and complete work accounting
Scale 1 uses the operator directly. For scale 4/16/64, continuous values evaluate four absolute-world coarse anchors and add interpolation work; conservative work is `4*base_work + 64`. Categories and booleans select one exact nearest anchor, with lower-anchor half ties, so work is `base_work + 64`. Recursive input costs already include their own scales, transforms and derivative stencils. The total graph charge is the sum for every published/declared expanded node; caching never reduces the admission bound. Geometry compilation records owned point bytes and segment query costs. Region assignment records configured preparation work and fixed bounded solver scratch, in addition to prepared solution storage. Subgraph validation/expansion and immutable input preparation are bounded independently from per-cell sampling. The compiler's `preparation_operations`, `preparation_bytes` and per-node/graph sampling costs are inspectable through the native API. These are explicit capacity contracts rather than performance claims. The preparation-work ledger starts at 1,024 units, charges 256 per authored node, 512 per subgraph declaration, `256+64*points` per geometry, and the full configured work allowance for every assignment. Actual/validation expansion additionally charges 512 per instance call and 8,192 per expanded node. The compiler validates unused templates under the same shared ledger. The 1,024-instance-call ceiling prevents empty expansions from evading node limits. The conservative memory ledger includes compiled node capacity, bounded expansion/declaration storage, caller scratch, copied geometry and the fixed 256 KiB solver scratch per assignment. It is checked before graph expansion or solver preparation; it is a conservative allowance, not measured heap residency.

Section: Procedural Deepworks qualification and visual review > How are cost and performance claims reported?
GEN-007's bounded candidate indices accelerate sampling by identifying nearby grammar features, routes and projections. They preserve canonical record order and still use the original geometry/mask tests. Index creation is charged to preparation work and memory. Conservative logical charges remain explicit and must fit declared recipe limits; the indices do not authorize unbounded output. The recipe declares at most 4,000,000,000 logical operations for a whole four-plane bundle, 16,000,000,000 for generic final-raster validation, 16 MiB of charged plane-plan storage and 64 MiB of publication data. The four qualified seeds fit those limits. Native grammar storage and plane-plan storage are separate charges; neither is process memory. Seed 19337 leaves only about 0.8% of the plane-operation budget despite four unused template slots. New seeds or denser edits can receive an explicit bounded refusal and require fresh qualification. Report actual local generation, validation and preview durations separately from logical units. Include compiler/runtime, OS/CPU, renderer, resolution, seed, worker/slice settings and peak-memory measurement method. A charged-operation heatmap is an estimate; a measured-chunk-time heatmap is local timing at chunk resolution. Neither establishes target-PC performance or per-cell timing. The declared process envelope is **2 GiB for headless qualification/reactions** and **4 GiB for graphical execution**. The original provisional 2 GiB graphical bound failed during cold Mesa rendering and remains a retained failure. The cold/warm difference is consistent with renderer initialization and shader-cache overhead; the measurements do not attribute the peak to a particular allocation. The final canonical software-renderer run uses `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1`, `LP_NUM_THREADS=2` and `GALLIVM_PERF=nopt`; its fresh XDG/Mesa-cache peak fits the revised 4 GiB envelope. Cold and warm timing/RSS records, Godot static allocation peak, native charged storage and their different scopes are retained in the [audit](../audits/2026-10-21-gen007-workbench-qualification.md) and [raw evidence directory](../audits/gen007/). The Linux process wrapper records the maximum child/descendant RSS, not aggregate simultaneous process-tree memory.

Generation retains its private pending material/diagnostic arrays; cancellation or failure discards both payloads and their receipt hashes. A ready chunk is one complete result. Compilation, preparation and per-chunk rejection are not permission to expose a partially generated map.

Section: Typed spatial fields, transforms and reusable generation graphs > Which derivatives and geometric detectors are defined?
Spacing `h` is explicitly `1..64` cells. The first derivative uses centered differences, for example `(f(x+h,y)−f(x−h,y))/(2h)`. Second derivatives use the centered three-point form. The mixed derivative uses four diagonal samples. All positions are absolute-world coordinates of immutable functions. A chunk boundary is not a stencil boundary; it cannot substitute missing neighbor data or change the answer. | Operator | Numerical meaning | |---|---| | `gradient` | `(fx, fy)` with input unit exponent minus one | | `slope` | `hypot(fx,fy)`; nonnegative, same units as gradient | | `aspect` | `atan2(fy,fx)`, in signed radians; zero gradient has a finite zero convention | | `divergence` | `dVx/dx + dVy/dy` | | `curl` | Scalar `dVy/dx − dVx/dy`; positive sign is fixed by this formula | | `ridge`, `valley` | `max(0,−laplacian)` and `max(0,laplacian)`; input exponent minus two | | `local_minimum`, `local_maximum` | Strict comparison to the four axial samples, producing an exact boolean; a plateau is not a strict extremum | | `curvature` | Level-set curvature `(fxx*fy²−2*fxy*fx*fy+fyy*fx²)/hypot(fx,fy)^3`; zero at zero gradient, units `cells^-1` | Finite differences approximate nonlinear functions and discontinuities. The analytical regression uses quadratic scalar fields, radial circle distance and linear vector fields to establish values, signs and units independently. These operators detect properties of the authored function; they are not a fluid solver, a proof of physical traversability or exact geometry reconstruction.

Section: Typed spatial fields, transforms and reusable generation graphs > How are coordinate transforms composed?
`transform` samples its source in local coordinates. For local point `q`, world point `p`, origin `o`, translation `t`, rotation `R`, shear `H` and anisotropic scale `S`, the convention is: ```text p = o + t + R H S (q − o) q = o + (R H S)^−1 (p − o − t) H = [[1, shear_x], [shear_y, 1]] S = diag(sx, sy) ``` Positive angles use the ordinary coordinate rotation matrix. World y is the generator's downward-positive axis, so the on-screen visual interpretation follows that axis convention. Translation and origin are positions in cells; angles are radians. Nested transforms compose through explicit source inputs and are bounded by graph depth and recursive sampling work. `transform_vector` samples its vector source at the original point and applies the **forward linear part** `R H S`. It does not add translation or origin. Coordinate deformation of a vector field and transformation of its vector values are therefore separate operations an author may compose deliberately. The compiler rejects zero/tiny scales, singular shears, nonfinite parameters and excessive declared bounds. Translation, rotation/reflection and uniform scale preserve an exact SDF. A uniform scale multiplies the sampled distance by the absolute scale. Anisotropic scaling or shear preserves the zero set but changes the result to a general implicit scalar. Its reported minimum/maximum distance factors are the affine matrix's singular-value bounds: multiplying the absolute local distance by those factors bounds the world distance to the transformed boundary. General warps, polar maps and coarse interpolation discard an exact-distance claim. Do not use a warped scalar as an exact clearance radius. `repeat` subtracts its phase origin and maps each axis into local `[0,period)` using floor-equivalent remainder. `mirror` folds the phase-shifted, period-doubled axis into local `[0,period]`. Negative inputs and exact seams obey the same rules as positive inputs. These coordinate maps repeat a function; they do not imply that material routes connect across the repeated boundary. `polar` samples its source at `(radius/radial_scale, angle/angular_scale)`; `log_polar` replaces the first component with `log(max(radius,min_radius)/radial_scale)`. Both measure radius/angle relative to an explicit origin. Angle uses `atan2`, with angle zero at the origin; the negative-x, zero-y branch is positive pi. Radial/angular scales map physical radius/radians into the source's sampling coordinates. The logarithm's minimum-radius clamp and angle branch seam are explicit numerical conventions, independent of resident chunks. `warp` takes `[source, displacement_vector]`; the displacement is sampled at the original point and radially capped to `max_displacement` cells before resampling the source. Repeated composition is bounded; no neighbor-generation recursion is introduced. Public samples use integer world coordinates in `[-2^40,2^40)`. Internal transformed,

Section: Procedural spatial operator inventory > Interpolation and complete work accounting
Scale 1 uses the operator directly. For scale 4/16/64, continuous values evaluate four absolute-world coarse anchors and add interpolation work; conservative work is `4*base_work + 64`. Categories and booleans select one exact nearest anchor, with lower-anchor half ties, so work is `base_work + 64`. Recursive input costs already include their own scales, transforms and derivative stencils. The total graph charge is the sum for every published/declared expanded node; caching never reduces the admission bound. Geometry compilation records owned point bytes and segment query costs. Region assignment records configured preparation work and fixed bounded solver scratch, in addition to prepared solution storage. Subgraph validation/expansion and immutable input preparation are bounded independently from per-cell sampling. The compiler's `preparation_operations`, `preparation_bytes` and per-node/graph sampling costs are inspectable through the native API. These are explicit capacity contracts rather than performance claims. The preparation-work ledger starts at 1,024 units, charges 256 per authored node, 512 per subgraph declaration, `256+64*points` per geometry, and the full configured work allowance for every assignment. Actual/validation expansion additionally charges 512 per instance call and 8,192 per expanded node. The compiler validates unused templates under the same shared ledger. The 1,024-instance-call ceiling prevents empty expansions from evading node limits. The conservative memory ledger includes compiled node capacity, bounded expansion/declaration storage, caller scratch, copied geometry and the fixed 256 KiB solver scratch per assignment. It is checked before graph expansion or solver preparation; it is a conservative allowance, not measured heap residency.

Section: Hierarchical procedural places and structural routes > How do finite planning regions own cross-chunk places?
`region_size` anchors a square lattice at world zero. `region_window` is `[region_x, region_y, width, height]` in **region addresses**, not cells. A window is finite and explicit; each of its regions independently constructs the same regional hierarchy. A feature belongs to its parent region and must fit that region through recursively contained parent bounds. It may span many storage chunks. A chunk samples that immutable plan even if the chunk containing the feature origin has never been requested. The planning window is not part of a regional identity. Compiling one region, a larger window containing it, or disjoint neighboring windows therefore uses the same local identities, geometry and ownership. Storage chunk size, request order, worker completion and budget slicing cannot choose a feature owner. Cross-region structures in this version are explicit route/service connections; arbitrary building boxes crossing their canonical region are rejected. There is no recursive expansion beyond the finite declared window and no hidden neighbor publication requirement. Each region has a center hub with four explicit orthogonal passage arms. A shared boundary key is `<world>/grid<size>/boundary/x/<boundary-x>/<region-y>` for a vertical edge, or `<world>/grid<size>/boundary/y/<region-x>/<boundary-y>` for a horizontal edge. The world seed and that key select a port within the middle third of the edge. Both neighbors produce the same aperture position, width, type and canonical owner. The west or north region owns the shared record; it may lie outside the requested window. Regional local ports refer to that shared record, and duplicate shared records are checked and deduplicated within a multi-region plan. `secondary_loop` adds a rectangular loop at one-quarter/three-quarter region coordinates and an explicit link to the hub. `service_trunk` places a horizontal service route at `region_size/4 - 8`; `liquid_trunk` places a liquid route at `3*region_size/4 + 8`. Their material and route type are declared. They are semantic service access paths, not proofs of simulated flow or an unbroken pressure network. Service/liquid ports use the same west-owner canonical boundary rule with their route type in the key. Required empty passages retain raster precedence over service material where the two intersect.

Choose the world namespace, canonical region size/window and stable feature rule IDs. Give each complex, room and apparatus a contained rectangle. For each feature, decide its responsibility on play, rear, atmosphere and far. Add projections that point back to that feature or a canonical regional route. Use a shell for architectural mass, a fill for a solid part or explicit opening, and an omission with a reason for intentional empty space. Per-plane overrides are world-space authoring data; a presentation offset does not replace geometry. Keep passage carving later than surrounding structure and retain final hard material overrides. Recheck projected play materials after any blocking change. Use the existing [building material catalogue](../systems/building-material-catalogue.md). Simplify them or author a smaller finite region; do not raise limits without measuring the resulting publication.

Section: ADR-013: Canonical semantic generation before rasterization > Why this boundary?
Request-order ownership would make neighboring chunks disagree when produced independently. A mutable shared global plan would add synchronization, lifetime and streaming obligations before the programme's streaming stage. Recursive neighbor planning would lack a finite dependency footprint. Canonical regions and shared boundary records provide independently reproducible discovery while keeping the plan's work and memory finite. Semantic identity and content receipts answer different questions. The former identifies a place across unrelated edits; the latter detects changed geometry, material or constraints. Declaration order and recipe revisions therefore do not rename surviving places. Changing the region grid explicitly changes the identity namespace instead of silently moving an old place to a new owner. Curve order supplies a repeatable structural sequence. It cannot certify a physical path, especially for Morton jumps or repeated finite tiles. Routes use explicit rectilinear geometry and compatible sockets. Final raster validation then checks Empty-cell clearance/connectivity for the declared floating square profile, including independently authored shared apertures. Final support qualification separately checks retained solid contact along declared floor/ceiling/wall edges, with partial-contact diagnostics. Neither profile claims post-simulation structural stability or controller performance.

Section: Chunk, tile, and buffer model > How does a generation chunk relate to simulation geometry?
**Current GEN-001/GEN-002 source:** an opt-in [`generation::Recipe`](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) chooses the square output partition for a procedural proposal. Sampling uses global coordinates, so requesting neighboring chunks in a different order or partitioning the same region does not change its material proposals. Generation neither runs the scheduler nor reads which neighbors happen to be resident. Flow Network and District Grammar derive shared macrocell ports from seed and global topology independently of output chunk size. Theme/brush changes cannot change that topology parameter locally; modules run before the connective skeleton is restored, while a final hard material override can intentionally close a route. These are generated layout relationships, not simulation write domains or new cellular transfer rules. The [generation contract](../systems/procedural-world-generation.md) owns their bounds/precedence; World admission separately requires its configured chunk size and a previously absent destination. Finite Hilbert/Morton tiles, aggregate grains, mask shapes and output chunks are separate spatial partitions. GEN-002 addresses each from absolute coordinates with signed floor division; changing output chunk size does not reset a field tile or grain. Consecutive Hilbert ranks connect only within one finite tile, while Morton ranks are not a continuous route. Neither substitutes for the generator's macrocell port network or the simulation scheduler's write domains. See the [field/curve contract](../systems/procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md). GEN-004 adds a finite authored window of canonical world-zero region addresses. Its `region_size` defines semantic ownership independently of output chunks; changing that grid size intentionally changes the semantic identity namespace. A region-owned building can span many storage chunks. Neighboring regions derive the same shared boundary socket without observing chunk residency, and explicit passages and utility routes carry the cross-region connection. The [hierarchy contract](../systems/procedural-hierarchical-generation.md) distinguishes these finite plans from future persistent-world streaming.

Section: Procedural world generation candidates > What is implemented?
**Current candidate source, GEN-001 / [#163](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/163) and GEN-002 / [#171](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/171):** three CPU procedural generators share one immutable recipe, theme hierarchy, spatial control stack and extensible native feature registry. They produce actual material IDs for signed-coordinate chunks. Generation is separate from simulation: it does not tick materials, query a mutable World, call Godot, request neighboring chunks or share a mutable random generator. The [public native API](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) and [implementation](../../native/src/world_generation.cpp) own these semantics. GEN-002 adds named structured-noise/finite-curve fields, scalar sidechains, masked context-aware guidance and sculpting, aggregate material recipes and paced diagnostic channels. The focused [fields and modifiers contract](procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md) owns those controls, immutable initial context and finite Hilbert/Morton scope. GEN-003 / [#190](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/190) adds explicit schema-2 [typed spatial functions](procedural-typed-spatial-fields.md): signed distance/vector/category values, transformed/derived geometry, reusable parameter subgraphs, structured seeds, finite adjacency assignments and world-aligned multiresolution sampling. The retained scalar graph remains separately defined; typed spatial functions have no per-cell initial-context input. Only explicit normalized `spatial:<id>` outputs may drive existing masks and mappings. GEN-004 / [#191](https://github.com/techrote/cybersand/issues/191) adds explicit schema-3 [hierarchical semantic plans](procedural-hierarchical-generation.md). Finite canonical regions own nested places and cross-chunk structures; stable rule/slot IDs, placement constraints, matched sockets, explicit loops/service trunks and final-raster route reports precede ordinary chunk publication. Selected immutable semantic geometries may feed the typed graph. The hierarchy does not add World streaming or replace final hard material authority. | Candidate | Generated structure | Suitable starting point | |---|---|---| | `strata` | Smoothly varying surface, domain-warped caves, strata, deposits and material-specific deep fill | Organic terrain, underground spaces and theme transitions | | `flow_network` | Strata plus a connected macrocell hub/port network, carved after structural modules | Interconnected passages, service routes and excavation networks | | `district_grammar` | Global room/floor lattice with repeated doors and accents, plus the same hub/port network | Dense urban interiors, industrial districts and structured construction | ![Actual native generation with the same authored controls across the three candidates](../figures/worldgen-candidates.png) Seed 314159; each panel covers 512 by 384 cells at origin `[-256,0]`. Reproduce the material pixels with `make worldgen-demo`. This is generation output, before simulation. Every candidate consumes the same brushes, paths, overrides and feature instances. A hard candidate override can choose another generator inside a rectangular zone. This is deliberately a set of provisional algorithms, not a selected production world style or a proof of useful player navigation. In particular, generator connectivity does not establish actor clearance, gravity traversal or fluid equilibrium; the existing material and actor owners retain those semantics. **Current authoring surface:** the separate [worldgen workbench](../../godot/worldgen_workbench.tscn) previews generated material pixels and performs bounded demand generation while panning.

results.query: How are hard grammar occupancy, exact multiplicity, neighbor, support and socket constraints distinguished from weighted placement preferences and omission fallbacks?
facts: Rules run by descending priority then ID; finite candidate choices rank preferences, curve rank and ID before hard requirements filter them.
Occupancy is summed rule feature area divided by parent area, and count requests exact stable slots per parent.
Support/open volume, separation, required or forbidden sibling tags, exclusive families, service access and compatible sockets are checked as declared semantic constraints.
Rejected layouts fail transactionally; an authored omit fallback records the unmet requirement and removed features cannot satisfy later hard neighbors or support.
The bounded priority strategy may reject a feasible arrangement requiring earlier placement changes; it is not a complete packing solver.
Final static-solid-contact-v1 qualification is separate from semantic placement receipts and route clearance; each declared support requires at least one surviving final Solid contact.

Section: Hierarchical procedural places and structural routes > How do I author and inspect the multi-district example?
Load [`hierarchy-multi-district.json`](../../examples/worldgen/hierarchy-multi-district.json) through the Workbench hierarchy example control or `CyberWorldGenerator.configure`. It covers `[-128,-128,256,256]` cells in four canonical 128-cell regions, using 64-cell storage chunks. Each region contains semantic theme subdivisions, one 104×72 foundry, a 64×66 gallery, a machinery bay, an inspection dais with floor and wall constraints, a floor-mounted pump, a ceiling console and two embedded dais lights. The machinery bay occupies 22.22% of its foundry. Neighbor, separation, service, exact multiplicity, socket and occupancy constraints are authored data. The profile uses the shared finite assignment solver for district theme blends, order-1 Hilbert-ranked foundry candidates and detail placement, a real theme-boundary preference for a marker, explicit primary routes and secondary loops, a four-site curve-ordered service tour and straight service/liquid trunks, a prepared vault module, a weathered aggregate shell and a typed distance mask around an exported tour loop. Its Strata base is composed with Flow Network and District Grammar overrides. `get_semantic_plan()` exposes the hierarchy and receipts; `inspect_cell()` reports contribution provenance; `validate_routes()` reports the declared final-cell traversal and support-contact qualifications separately. The example deliberately places its compact apparatus away from both semantic passage footprints and the existing candidate macro network for the authored seed. Its retained qualification and the footprint inspection are recorded in the [dated audit](../audits/2026-10-21-gen004-hierarchical-generation.md). For a new place, choose its canonical region/window and stable rule IDs first. Declare parent-relative candidate rectangles and exact counts, then add hard requirements and socket apertures. Give higher-priority scopes to required supports or theme areas. Add preferences only after a valid hard layout exists. Use explicit omission fallback only when absence is an acceptable authored outcome. Inspect semantic receipts before tuning masks/materials, then recheck final raster routes after any hard override. Save accepted JSON with full numeric precision using the existing Workbench configuration path. [`grammar-v1.schema.json`](../../examples/worldgen/schemas/grammar-v1.schema.json) is the versioned JSON authoring schema for the `grammar` member of a schema-3 recipe. The native compiler additionally checks relational, geometric, type, cycle, work and memory invariants that JSON Schema cannot establish. The [build guide](../operations/local-build-and-validation.md#hierarchical-generation-example-and-acceptance) routes executable tests. Human movement feel, Windows/browser behavior and render throughput require their own dated execution evidence.

Section: Hierarchical procedural places and structural routes > How are hard constraints and preferences resolved?
Rules under one parent run in descending priority, with lexical rule ID breaking ties. A rule requests an exact `count`; each slot considers distinct authored candidate rectangles relative to the parent. Candidates rank by weighted preference score, then finite-curve rank, then candidate ID. Hard constraints filter this ordered list. Candidate rejection reasons are retained. This is a bounded, deterministic priority placement strategy: a feasible arrangement that would require moving an earlier high-priority placement may be rejected. There is no claim of complete search over all possible layouts. | Declaration | Exact semantic check | |---|---| | `intersects_route` | Candidate intersects an explicit regional passage footprint. Curve succession does not satisfy it. | | `minimum_separation` | Euclidean distance between sibling rectangle extents is at least the greater of their two requested separations. | | `floor`, `ceiling`, `wall` | Candidate contacts the corresponding declared solid parent interior surface or a previously placed solid sibling surface. A separate final-cell report checks whether a solid contact survives rasterization; neither check models stability after simulation. | | `open_volume` | Candidate fits inside a shelled parent's interior and does not overlap a sibling for which either side requires open volume. Ancestors are not competing siblings. | | `service` | A declared `service` or `liquid` route lies within `neighbor_distance` of the candidate rectangle. This is bounded geometric access, not liquid dynamics. | | `occupancy_min/max` | Sum of this rule's placed sibling rectangle areas divided by parent rectangle area falls in the inclusive range. It is a semantic area quota, distinct from aggregate material weights. | | `count` | Exactly this many stable slots are placed per parent unless an authored omission fallback records an exception. Candidate IDs are not reused within the same rule instance. | | `required_neighbors`, `forbidden_neighbors` | Named sibling tags are present/absent within `neighbor_distance`; final checks see all siblings, including later declarations. | | `exclusive_family` | At most one placed sibling occupies the named family. | | `minimum_sockets`, `maximum_sockets`, `connected` | Counts stay within the declared range; connected features have a compatible attached passage socket. Required socket matches are mechanically checked. | | `allowed_materials` | Declared shell/interior and integrated aggregate contributions must obey the feature's declared material set; an empty set imposes no feature-local material filter. Final hard overrides retain their separate authority. | Preferences are weighted, finite scores for closeness to a route, parent floor, ceiling or wall, a boundary between two selected semantic sibling themes, or progressive finite-curve density. Theme-boundary scoring uses already established sibling feature geometry and theme records; use higher-priority

Section: ADR-013: Canonical semantic generation before rasterization > Decision
GEN-004 compiles immutable semantic plans in a finite, authored window of world-zero-anchored regions. A region owns its feature hierarchy; each feature's identity combines the authored world namespace, grid size, signed region address, parent path, rule ID and stable slot. Storage chunks only sample the plan. Shared boundary ports use canonical west/north ownership and keys independent of the compilation window. Neighbor generation and worker completion never negotiate which feature wins. Routine place construction is declarative. Bounded authored candidates and deterministic rule priority provide layout decisions, with explicit hard constraints, weighted preferences, rejection and authored omission receipts. GEN-003's finite assignment solver remains the single categorical adjacency solver. Trusted native modules remain an extension point within the established generation stack. The [hierarchy contract](../systems/procedural-hierarchical-generation.md) owns the executable vocabulary and precise scope. The planner supports region-contained buildings crossing storage chunks and explicit route/service structures crossing region boundaries. It does not admit arbitrary region-spanning building boxes or claim complete geometric constraint search.

Section: Hierarchical procedural places and structural routes > How are sockets, routes and finite curves used structurally?
A socket has an authored ID, route type, outward direction, integer edge offset, odd aperture width, required flag and attachment policy. Width and offset must fit the selected feature edge. Automatic attachment selects the nearest compatible predeclared regional route deterministically, checks passage width, creates an opposite-facing matching socket and an explicit connector that first exits along the authored normal. Shared boundary ports remain canonical records. Unsupported or unmatched required connections reject the plan. Hilbert, Morton and Peano are finite orderings of authored candidate addresses `order_x/order_y`. Their ranks affect candidate placement, progressive density and retained inspection/tour order. They can order declared district subdivisions or apparatus positions without array-order dependence. With `curve_services`, a bounded service tour visits finite curve sites in rank order and constructs explicit orthogonal material trunk edges between them, joined to the straight regional service. Hilbert/Morton use at most sixteen sites and Peano nine; a Morton jump is an authored L-shaped route, not an inferred adjacent step. Curve ranks never replace the explicit edge geometry used by hub arms, loops, utility trunks and socket connectors. Hilbert/Peano adjacency holds only inside their documented finite domains; Morton may jump. A sorted list of features alone is not a physical route.

Section: Procedural generation fields and masked modifiers > What do Hilbert and Morton guarantee at signed chunk boundaries?
Curve tiles have side `2^order`, where `order` is an integer from 1 through 20. Each local curve cell covers `cell_size` world cells per axis, an integer from 1 through 4096. Origin coordinates are integer cells. At the maximum settings, one tile spans `2^32` world cells per axis; intermediate address arithmetic is wide enough for that extent. `curve_address(kind, x, y, order, cell_size, origin_x, origin_y)` returns signed tile coordinates, local unsigned coordinates and a local rank. Floor division assigns negative cells consistently. `curve_index` and `curve_point` convert between local coordinates and rank without sampling any neighbor. Scalar curve fields divide the rank by `2^(2*order)-1`, retaining exact endpoint values. Hilbert order 1 visits `(0,0)`, `(0,1)`, `(1,1)`, `(1,0)`. Consecutive Hilbert ranks share an edge **within the same finite tile**. Tiling repeats that local addressing pattern; there is no promised continuous infinite Hilbert path between tiles. Morton interleaves x bits in even lanes and y bits in odd lanes; successive Morton ranks need not share an edge. A Morton field is therefore a spatial ordering control, not an automatically connected corridor. The generator's separately defined macrocell hub/port network owns interconnected routes. Curve fields may guide material seams, masks, variation or parameter mapping without replacing that connectivity contract. Both curve ranks and resulting material proposals stay independent of output chunk size, including partitions and brush shapes crossing negative coordinates. Samples must lie inside `[-2^40,2^40)`; curve and field origin parameters accept both endpoints of `[-2^40,2^40]`. Out-of-domain requests and invalid curve ranks, local coordinates, orders or cell sizes reject explicitly.

Section: Chunk, tile, and buffer model > How does a generation chunk relate to simulation geometry?
**Current GEN-001/GEN-002 source:** an opt-in [`generation::Recipe`](../../native/include/cybersand/world_generation.hpp) chooses the square output partition for a procedural proposal. Sampling uses global coordinates, so requesting neighboring chunks in a different order or partitioning the same region does not change its material proposals. Generation neither runs the scheduler nor reads which neighbors happen to be resident. Flow Network and District Grammar derive shared macrocell ports from seed and global topology independently of output chunk size. Theme/brush changes cannot change that topology parameter locally; modules run before the connective skeleton is restored, while a final hard material override can intentionally close a route. These are generated layout relationships, not simulation write domains or new cellular transfer rules. The [generation contract](../systems/procedural-world-generation.md) owns their bounds/precedence; World admission separately requires its configured chunk size and a previously absent destination. Finite Hilbert/Morton tiles, aggregate grains, mask shapes and output chunks are separate spatial partitions. GEN-002 addresses each from absolute coordinates with signed floor division; changing output chunk size does not reset a field tile or grain. Consecutive Hilbert ranks connect only within one finite tile, while Morton ranks are not a continuous route. Neither substitutes for the generator's macrocell port network or the simulation scheduler's write domains. See the [field/curve contract](../systems/procedural-generation-fields-and-modifiers.md). GEN-004 adds a finite authored window of canonical world-zero region addresses. Its `region_size` defines semantic ownership independently of output chunks; changing that grid size intentionally changes the semantic identity namespace. A region-owned building can span many storage chunks. Neighboring regions derive the same shared boundary socket without observing chunk residency, and explicit passages and utility routes carry the cross-region connection. The [hierarchy contract](../systems/procedural-hierarchical-generation.md) distinguishes these finite plans from future persistent-world streaming.

Section: Hierarchical procedural places and structural routes > How does a semantic plan become material cells? > What does floating-square route validation prove after a hard override?
`validate_routes()` checks **final rasterized cells**, after fields, modules, aggregates and hard overrides, for an explicitly declared odd square clearance. This is the `floating-square-v1` geometric profile with four-neighbor connectivity. At the finite window edge, footprint checks are clipped to the canonical shared aperture; the report explicitly sets `boundary_apertures`. Independently planned opposite halves complete that aperture, and stitched boundary controls are required to establish the full crossing. It does not model gravity, jumps, a particular articulated actor, controllers or material motion after simulation. An authored hard override can intentionally block a required route: material output preserves the override and the route report records failure. A blocked report must not be described as successful traversal. No abstract graph result substitutes for this final-cell check. For a semantic-plane recipe, additional projections can subsequently change material. The [GEN-007 qualification oracle](../operations/procedural-qualification.md#how-are-routes-checked-after-all-material-decisions) therefore checks the final projected play plane independently, with the same distinction between geometric clearance and actor traversal. The same report separately exposes `supports_passed` for the `static-solid-contact-v1` profile. For each declared floor, ceiling or wall constraint it inspects final material cells immediately outside the feature's rectangle. A check passes when at least one inspected cell has `MaterialState::Solid`; the wall check inspects both vertical sides. It retains checked/missing counts, the first missing coordinate and the feature/constraint identity. Partial contact can therefore pass, and `passed` still means the route profile alone. A consumer requiring both qualifications must inspect both booleans. This catches total removal of a required support by routes, modules, modifiers or final overrides. It does not establish that the whole apparatus survived, that its support spans the entire footprint, that the solid is itself grounded, or that the resulting assembly remains stable after simulation. Cell provenance and fixture-specific raster controls are needed for those stronger claims.

Section: Semantic four-plane generation and bounded interlayer contracts > How are planes projected and rasterized?
A plane policy declares its uncovered material, rate, whether play consumes the existing generator, and an explanation of intentionally empty space. Only play may use `base_generator`. A projection template selects an authored grammar rule or `$region`, chooses a plane, and references `feature` or `routes` geometry. Feature projections use the canonical rectangle, or an explicitly contained feature-relative rectangle. Route projections reuse a region's actual passage, service or liquid polyline and its width; an override must remain bounded. `fill` paints the selected geometry. `shell` uses explicit wall/interior material and thickness. `omit` preserves an explicit composition decision and reason. Material overrides use ordinary valid native IDs; material 10 remains invalid. Density is a deterministic feature/coordinate mask in absolute world space. Optional `application` and `exclusion` reference the same immutable GEN-003 graph as `spatial:<expanded.id>`. Only dimensionless normalized or boolean outputs are admitted; raw scalar, distance, vector and category outputs need an explicit typed conversion. Effective density is `density * application * (1 - exclusion)`, with absent masks equal to one/zero. The shared graph is evaluated once per affected plane and coordinate, charged to raster work, and its transitive input identity is retained in projection revisions. Both examples share a weathering field between rear and far geometry. Ascending priority and stable projection ID determine raster precedence. Final play hard-material overrides remain final. An authored empty passage projection can deliberately carve the semantic route through decorative geometry. Every region needs explicit atmosphere and far-plane projection records, even when the intended composition is empty. Per-feature omissions are not runtime permissions. Static appearance is produced by the existing material renderer, not by generated bitmap textures or a second material catalogue. Parallax, pan, zoom and visibility live only in `CyberDepthCompositor`. They are absent from native schema input, seed selection, ownership and hashes. Admission translates absolute semantic coordinates into the local finite World only once; all retained IDs and geometry still refer to the absolute plan.

No field reads live World state or partial raster output, and normalized mask conversion remains explicit.
